Preface

Within the narrative and theoretical scope of the book, this appendix serves primarily to demonstrate how a memory-safe, C-successor language ought to define its semantic boundaries, rather than to provide a drop-in replacement for a rigorous ISO-level standard.

In this context, CobaltC can best be described as a systems language designed to address the safety problems of C while adopting a more robust structural model.

If nothing else, it illustrates the exact pain points and formal guarantees required to make a safe systems programming language actually function.

As argued throughout The Wrong Memory essays, attempting to tack a "safe subset" onto an inherently unsafe language usually fails because the core language semantics still allow invariant violations. By embedding ownership and borrowing into the core type system, CobaltC makes safety an intrinsic property of the language rather than an optional discipline imposed upon it.

CobaltC unashamedly draws on the ownership and memory-safety techniques demonstrated by Rust. Although Rust isn't the origin of most of these ideas, its significant contribution was demonstrating how they could be combined into a practical, high-performance systems language. CobaltC adopts that safety architecture without attempting to reproduce Rust's syntax or overall language philosophy. Instead, it applies the broader body of ideas to the problem identified in Appendix II: making semantic invariants such as ownership, lifetime, aliasing, mutability, and bounds properties that the compiler can represent and enforce, rather than obligations the programmer must maintain by convention.

The CobaltC Proposition

The distinction is perhaps easiest to see in a deliberately small example. Allocate some storage, keep a second name for it, destroy the storage, and use the second name.

C accepts this program without complaint — GCC and Clang compile it silently even with every common warning enabled. At best, a modern compiler may warn about a case this obvious; move the free behind one function call and the warning disappears, while the bug does not. The program compiles, runs, and reads the wrong memory. The fact that alias still refers to freed storage exists only in the programmer's head.

C

"You have the power. Don't screw it up."

The same program, the same shape — allocate, alias, destroy, use — and it does not run. The fact that alias still points into data lives in the language, so destroying data underneath it is refused before the program starts, with a named diagnostic: heuristic warnings on one side, a semantic guarantee on the other.

CobaltC

"You have the power. Let’s prove you’re exercising it correctly."

The guarantee is not bought by removing capability. Below, two exclusive (mutable) references into the same array are held at once — something safety-minded languages commonly refuse — legal here because the compiler has proven they touch disjoint elements. CobaltC forbids the crime, not the capability.

CobaltC retains the same fine-grained control, while allowing the compiler to establish the relevant safety properties: a and b refer to distinct elements of values, their mutable accesses are disjoint, and the underlying storage remains owned by values.

This guide describes the CobaltC specification, edition 2026.102201.

Introduction

Why CobaltC exists, what it promises, and which features were chosen to keep those promises.

What CobaltC is

CobaltC is a small systems programming language with a C-family surface syntax. It is designed around one idea: the facts that correct low-level code depends on should live in the language, not in the programmer's memory. When you write C, you have to remember that a pointer is still valid, that an integer cannot overflow here, that a buffer has been initialised, that nobody else is writing to that struct right now, and that this handle is closed exactly once. CobaltC's goal is that every such fact is either represented and checked by the language, or explicitly marked as trusted by you.

CobaltC is not a safe language obtained by removing low-level capability. You still get deterministic control over resources, raw storage, foreign functions, threads, and predictable data layout. What changes is that each of those capabilities comes with a precise account of what is checked, when it is checked, and what you are asserting when the language cannot check it.

The two implementations: coby and cobc

CobaltC ships with two implementations, both written in Rust, and they share one front end — the same parser, name resolution and static checks — so they accept and reject exactly the same programs, with the same diagnostics.

coby is the reference interpreter. It runs a program straight from its source on the abstract machine the specification defines, performing every check the specification requires on every operation. It is the specification's meaning made executable: when this guide says a program prints something or stops with a diagnostic, that is what coby does. There is no build step, so it is the quickest way to run a program or try an idea.

cobc is the native compiler. After the shared front end has checked the program, it translates it to plain C and compiles that with the system's C compiler (GCC or Clang) against cbrt, its run-time library. A compiled program keeps every run-time check the specification requires except those the compiler proves can never fail — the rest becomes ordinary C — so it runs many times faster than the interpreter while behaving identically. cobc --keep-c leaves the generated C beside the executable if you want to read what your program became; Reading the C that cobc generates, below, says what is in it and what you can do with it.

The two are kept honest against each other: the test suites require cobc's executables to match coby's output and diagnostics byte for byte on every program, under both GCC and Clang — including every complete example in this guide. Use coby to run a program at once; use cobc to build an executable, or to see how fast the program can be.

A third program, cbc, is cobc written in CobaltC itself (the repository's impl/selfhost/, over a front end that is likewise coby's written in CobaltC). It takes the same options and writes the same C, byte for byte, for every program; built by cobc, it compiles its own source to that same C again, so CobaltC's compiler can rebuild itself without the Rust one (D-0276). Its programs are cobc's programs, but it compiles them many times more slowly, so the examples in this guide say cobc.

On Linux the two work side by side, and everything in this guide runs under either. On Windows, coby runs programs, the formatter cobfmt (below) runs there too, and cobc builds Windows programs with a MinGW-w64 GCC, there or from Linux with --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu (D-0255; the repository's README says how).

Toolchain
CobaltC's interpreter (coby) and compiler (cobc) are available here; the repository's README says how to build them.

The objectives

The language design was derived from a short list of objectives, in priority order. Where two objectives conflict, the earlier one wins.

  1. Preserve semantic invariants. Arithmetic stays in range, references point at live objects, a resource has exactly one owner, an object is initialised before it is read, two threads never race on one location, and external data is treated as a claim until validated.
  2. Safety of valid safe programs. A well-formed program that writes no unsafe block of its own cannot violate any of those invariants on any conforming implementation. The standard library's own bodies do use unsafe (a Vec writes its elements through a raw pointer); those blocks are the implementation's to keep true, each listed in the specification with the fact that justifies it, so they cost the program nothing (§20, Who asserts what). If the language cannot establish a fact, the operation is one of: statically rejected, dynamically checked, explicitly fallible (returns a Result or Option), explicitly trusted (inside unsafe), or simply not provided.
  3. Consistency and composability. A handful of mechanisms that combine cleanly, instead of many overlapping features. Every value-placing construct (declarations, arguments, fields, returns) follows one rule; every access (through a name, a field, an index, a reference) follows one rule.
  4. Formal precision and deterministic diagnostics. The specification is written as rules, so two implementations must reject exactly the same programs and report the same named diagnostic. Every error you see has a stable identifier such as diag.aliasing-conflict.
  5. A small language. Every feature starts as absent and must earn its place. The result is a language you can hold in your head: no traits, no inheritance, no exceptions, no implicit conversions, no operator overloading, no macros.
  6. Low-level capability. Raw pointers, manual allocation, FFI, threads, and defined representation are all available, gated by unsafe where the language cannot check them.

Which features were chosen, and why

Each mechanism in CobaltC exists because a specific invariant needed a home. The table below is the map from objective to feature; the rest of this guide explains each feature in turn.

Invariant to protectMechanism CobaltC providesWhere to read
Arithmetic stays in rangeInteger + - * and / % are checked: overflow is a fault, never silent wrap. Wrapping, saturating and checked_ families are explicit opt-ins. There are no implicit numeric conversions; widen, narrow, reinterpret and friends are named calls.§06
A resource is owned once and released onceResource types (anything that owns something, marked resource or containing a resource) have a single holder. Assigning or passing one moves it. The old name becomes stale. Destruction is automatic at scope end, in reverse order, running the type's drop destructor.§07
No conflicting simultaneous accessTwo reference modes: ref<T, shared> (read-only, any number) and ref<T, exclusive> (read and write, alone). Conflicts are checked at every use, so a stale or conflicting reference is always caught. There is no mut on variables: mutability is a property of the access path, not the binding.§08, §09
A reference never outlives what it points atReferences cannot be returned or stored beyond their referent's scope; the obvious cases are rejected at compile time, the rest at run time. Functions with one reference parameter may return a reference without annotations.§10
No read of uninitialised storageDefinite assignment: a variable must be written on every path before it is read. Aggregates are initialised whole.§11
Types mean what they sayNominal typing, no subtyping, no coercions. Generics are monomorphic: each use with concrete types becomes its own copy of the function, so there is no run-time type information; a type parameter's operations come from one of five built-in bounds. Type inference is local: auto infers from the initialiser, and generic arguments come from arguments or the expected type.§12
Evaluation order is definedStrict left-to-right evaluation everywhere. Blocks, if and match are expressions.§13, §14
Function interfaces carry the whole contractA by-value resource parameter takes ownership; a shared reference can only read; an exclusive reference can mutate but not destroy. Closures declare their captures and the language checks the list.§15
Aggregates are whole and exhaustiveStructs, fixed arrays and enums with payloads. Array indexing is bounds-checked. match must be exhaustive.§16
Names are unambiguousModules with export/import, private by default. Name resolution is a fixed, documented order.§17
Failure is never silentTwo channels only: a checked fault is fatal and unwinds destructors; recoverable errors are Result values with the ? operator. There is no catch.§18
Threads do not racespawn/join with owning handles; a mutex whose interior is reachable only through a lock guard. The same aliasing rules apply across threads. A fault in a spawned thread ends that thread alone and reaches its supervisor as a value; any wait can be cancelled; deadlocks are reported.§19
External data is a claim, not a factunsafe blocks record what you assert. rawptr<T>, reclaim, allocate and unsafe extern fn are the only doors to the outside, and FFI signatures are restricted to plain types.§20
A text literal is a value; owned text is a resourceA string literal "…" is a str: a copyable value like an integer, valid UTF-8 by construction, never owned or freed. printf writes one. Owned, growable text is String, a resource: moved, destroyed at scope end, built from a str (a literal written where a String is declared becomes one there) or validated from bytes.§21
The library proves the language is sufficientVec<T>, String and Rc<T> are written in CobaltC itself, using nothing the language does not give you.§21

What CobaltC deliberately leaves out

These are considered decisions, not gaps. Each one either duplicated an existing mechanism or would have hidden a semantic fact the language wants to keep visible.

  • Implicit conversions and subtyping. i32 and i64 never mix silently.
  • User-defined traits or bounds. A type parameter's operations come from six built-in bounds — eq, ordered, number, integer, clone, plain (§12) — and nothing else: there is no way to declare a new bound. Your own struct or enum satisfies clone alone, by its fields or its own T::clone; to compare or combine values of your own types in generic code, pass the operation in as a function value.
  • Exceptions. A fault terminates the program after running destructors; expected failure is a Result.
  • Garbage collection. Ownership and scope-end destruction are deterministic; Rc<T> is a library type.
  • Character literals, and indexing or slicing a str. A str is a whole value; its bytes are reached with str_byte, and a single byte is written b'a': a u8, or the wider unsigned type its context asks for (§06). A String is sliced into views, &s[i..j], and taken apart by String::split, find and chars (§21). Text that arrives from outside is still bytes until String::from_utf8 validates it.
  • Method-call syntax. A call names the function's owner and writes the borrow it takes: Vec::push(&mut v, x), never v.push(x). The mode of every access path is visible where the path is formed, and . means one thing, field access. This is final (CHG-0132): no receiver sugar, no uniform call syntax, no auto-borrowing dot, no chaining.
  • A mut qualifier on bindings, switch and goto, import … as renaming, partial initialisation, lifetime annotations, memory orders weaker than sequential consistency. std::sync's Atomic (§19) is sequentially consistent.

How to read this guide

The next section is a complete program you can read top to bottom to absorb the syntax. After that there is one section per chapter of the normative specification, numbered the same way (§06 to §22) so you can cross-reference. If you are new, a good order is: the tour, then §22 (syntax reference), then §06 onward. Each section ends with a short list of rules of thumb. A reader who wants the model behind the rules — the abstract state, how references are formed and end, the one conflict check, what is decided before a program runs and what while it runs, threads and the trust boundary — can read spec/OVERVIEW.md, a prose account of the specification that cites, paragraph by paragraph, the rules it explains.

Every code block that is a complete program has been run through both implementations, the reference interpreter coby and the native compiler cobc, which agree on every one. A green runs badge means it executes to completion; a red badge names the diagnostic the language reports for that program. Diagnostics are labelled static (the program is rejected before it runs) or dynamic (a checked fault at run time); where a check is static only when the operands are literal, both labels may appear in the text. Comments inside examples use ✓ for accepted lines and ✗ for rejected ones.

The language and its standard library are still moving: an edition may change what an earlier one accepted, and the specification's register says so in each such edition's row. When a part is offered as stable it is first a candidate for thirty days, then stable, and after that a program written against it keeps compiling and keeps doing what it did, apart from a repair that closes a soundness hole or a change announced a release ahead (spec/STABILITY.md).

Running a program

Save a program as a .cb file. coby program.cb interprets it; cobc --run program.cb compiles it to native code and runs it, and cobc -o program program.cb keeps the executable. Both take the program's entry file (it may name other files as modules, §17), both exit with status 0 when the program runs to completion, and both print a rejected program's diagnostic the same way and exit with status 1. coby --check program.cb (or cobc --check) runs only the checks made before a program starts, and prints the same diagnostic for a program they reject; nothing runs, so a program that reads input, writes files or serves the network can be checked without doing so. Given a directory, it checks every .cb file in it. A program's own item takes precedence over an imported one of the same name (§17): a struct Vec or fn min beside import std; hides std's silently; --warn-shadow, given first, makes either tool note each such name on standard error, with its file and line, and otherwise behave as before.

There is no project file and no build step besides these commands. A program that spans several files names them itself: module parser "./parser.cb"; loads a file as a module, its path relative to the file that says so (§17), and extern "./fast.c"; or extern "z"; links C code of the program's own or an installed library (§20). cobc main.cb then builds the whole program from that one file, and coby main.cb runs it, with nothing else to keep in step (D-0231).

Testing a program

Tests live beside the code they test, in unittest blocks: a block at the top level of a file or a module, with an optional name. A test sees the module's private items, and is checked every time the program is, so a test that no longer compiles stops the build at once. Nothing runs it until you ask for a test run.

coby port.cb runs the program as always. coby --unittest port.cb runs its tests instead of main, each in a thread of its own: a failed assert, or any other fault, is reported, and the next test still runs. cobc --unittest --run port.cb does the same with the compiled program, and reports it identically; cobc --unittest -o port_tests port.cb keeps the test program.

The exit status is 1 when a test failed, so a test run can gate a build. --unittest-filter TEXT runs only the tests whose name contains TEXT. A file that holds only a library and its tests needs no main. A /// comment on a test right after a function makes it that function's example in the generated documentation (D-0230).

All code in this guide uses Allman brace style (every opening brace on its own line) and four-space indentation. That is a documentation convention: CobaltC ignores whitespace between tokens, so any brace placement is equally valid.

cobfmt, the formatter, writes that style for you: cobfmt program.cb rewrites the file in place, cobfmt --backup src/ does every .cb file under src/ and keeps each changed file's previous contents as NAME.cb.format.bak, and cobfmt --check src/ only lists the files it would change (for a test or a commit hook). It changes layout and nothing else: indentation, braces, spacing, blank lines, the : of a match's arms and of a bitstruct's fields aligned in one column, and trailing comments kept in theirs. Before writing, it checks that the result is the same program token for token, so formatting can never change what a program does. It keeps your line breaks — a short if (n == 0) { return; } stays on one line, though a function's body always opens on its own line — and a line longer than 120 characters that holds a list of arguments, parameters or array elements is broken one item per line. --width N sets another width, and --no-wrap leaves every line as long as it is. cobfmt --help lists the rest. Like coby, cobfmt runs on Windows as well as Linux, and it keeps a file's Windows line endings (\r\n) as they are.

Reading the C that cobc generates

cobc does not produce machine code itself. Once the shared front end has checked your program, cobc translates it into one C file and hands that file to GCC or Clang, which builds the executable against libcbrt.a, the run-time library. Normally the C file is deleted afterwards; cobc --keep-c -o prog prog.cb keeps it as prog.c, beside prog (without -o, a.out gets a.c). Under --run without -o it lives in a temporary directory and is deleted with it. If the C compiler ever rejects the file, cobc keeps it whatever you asked and prints its path.

The file is the complete translation of your program, not an excerpt: nothing but libcbrt.a is needed to build it. Even a seven-line program comes to a few hundred lines, because the file carries everything it uses, in this order:

  • The run-time interface, cbrt.h, copied in at the top: the C declarations of every cb_… function the program calls.
  • /* ---- types ---- */: each struct, enum and generic instantiation as a C struct, each followed by a _Static_assert that its size and alignment are the ones the specification fixes. Vec<i32> becomes struct s_std__Vec_Li32_R.
  • /* ---- string literals ---- */: your text literals as byte arrays.
  • /* ---- functions ---- */: one C function for each function the program actually uses, std's included, and one copy per instantiation of a generic one (f_std__Vec__push_Li32_R is Vec::push for i32). Your main is f_main; every other function is static, so the C compiler may inline it where it is called.
  • Call thunks and type descriptors: what fn values and the run-time checks need to know about each type.
  • int main, last: it hands the program's arguments to the runtime and starts f_main.

Inside a function, the C follows your statements one by one, and every run-time check the specification requires is an explicit line, so you can see exactly which checks your code still pays for. This is printf("%v\n", v[0]); with v a Vec<i32> (without the #line directives described below):

Elsewhere you will meet cb_borrow, cb_read and cb_write (the access and aliasing checks of §08–§09), __builtin_add_overflow and its relatives (checked arithmetic, §06), and cb_frame_push, cb_stmt_push and their _pop partners (the bookkeeping that runs destructors at scope end). A check the compiler has proved can never fail is simply absent.

Each line of C made from one of your statements is preceded by a directive such as #line 7 "prog.cb", which tells the C compiler which line of your file the next line of C came from. The C compiler's own messages, a debugger and a sanitizer then name prog.cb:7 rather than a line of prog.c; code made for std keeps the C file's own numbering. cobc --no-line-directives leaves the directives out, for reading the C on its own terms.

What you can do with it

  • Read it to see how a construct is compiled, which checks a loop costs, or why one way of writing it is faster than another. Performance (chapter P) collects what such reading and measuring found.
  • Build it yourself, with your own flags. cobc's own build of prog.c is the command below, and cobc -v prints the exact one it runs, with the real path of libcbrt.a (and any extern C file's compilation), ready to paste and change; -O2 is the default level and libcbrt.a sits beside the cobc executable. Add -g -O0 for a build to step through in a debugger, -fsanitize=address,undefined to have the sanitizers watch it, -march=native or -flto, or leave out -w to see the C compiler's warnings, which cobc silences.
  • Debug it. cobc -O0 -g prog.cb compiles with debug information and keeps it in the executable; gdb prog then stops at and steps through the lines of prog.cb, and a sanitizer build (--cc naming a wrapper that adds -fsanitize=address) reports a memory error in unsafe code at its .cb line. perf annotate shows the C beside them.
  • Report a compiler bug. If GCC or Clang rejects the generated C, that kept file and the C compiler's message are the whole report.

Keep -std=gnu11 and the two -f flags when you change the rest; each is part of the program's meaning. -ffp-contract=off stops the C compiler fusing a * b + c into one fused multiply-add with a single rounding, since the specification rounds each operation on its own (§06). -fno-optimize-sibling-calls keeps every call a real call, so a recursion too deep for the stack stops with the same diagnostic it gets from coby, instead of being turned into a loop that runs to completion. A program that links its own C code (extern "./mine.c";, §20) also needs that code compiled and added before -lcbrt; cobc -v shows both commands. The last two options only make the executable smaller: they leave out the parts of the runtime the program does not use, and the runtime's debug information (a hello world is about 0.8 MB with them, 5.9 MB without); drop them if you link a -g build to debug. cobc -s also leaves out the symbol table (--strip-all in place of --strip-debug, about 0.6 MB), which only profilers and debuggers read.

Watch out
The generated C is for reading and experimenting, not for keeping or editing by hand. Its names are internal and change between versions of cobc, and it is only correct with the libcbrt.a built alongside the same cobc. cobc refuses a mismatched runtime, but a build by hand skips that check.

Why compile to C

Compiling through C is a long tradition rather than a shortcut: C++ began as Cfront, which translated it into C, and Nim, Vala, Cython and several Scheme compilers work this way today. Few compilers write machine code entirely on their own; most hand the last step to a shared back end such as LLVM or GCC's. C as the target brings:

  • Portability for free. Wherever there is a C compiler, the language can run.
  • Decades of optimisation for free. GCC's and Clang's -O2 do register allocation, inlining, vectorisation and instruction scheduling better than a young compiler could.
  • Readable output. You can see what your program became, which is what --keep-c is for; LLVM IR or assembly would be far harder to read.
  • Easy C interoperation. Calling C functions and linking C libraries is natural, which is what unsafe extern fn (§20) needs.

What it costs

  • C's own rules come along. The generated C must avoid C's undefined behaviour, and it has to keep up as C compilers grow stricter: code an older compiler accepted with a warning, a newer one may reject outright.
  • Less control. Some things C cannot say directly (exact stack layout, particular calling conventions, precise debug information), so they are worked around with flags such as -ffp-contract=off above.
  • Slower builds. Every build includes a full C compilation.
  • Debuggers show C lines, not CobaltC lines. cobc emits no #line directives, so gdb steps through the C; the cb_at(file, line) calls lead back to your source.

For CobaltC the trade is a good one. Its central promise is that coby and cobc behave identically, and letting GCC and Clang do the machine-code work leaves cobc free to get the semantics and the checks exactly right.

A tour in one program

A complete, runnable program that introduces the syntax and the main capabilities, and the mistakes the compiler stops, before the reference sections begin.

Here is a complete program. Read it once for the shape of the syntax; every construct it uses has its own section later. It runs under both the interpreter and the compiler and prints the output shown below the code.

What the compiler stops

The program above is correct, so it shows what CobaltC lets you write. Just as much of the language is what it will not let through. Each of these mistakes, a one-line change to the same kind of code, is rejected before the program runs, by both the interpreter and the compiler, with a diagnostic that names the rule; what cannot be decided in advance is checked while the program runs, and stops it at the line where it happens (§08–§10).

Reading a diagnostic

Both tools report a mistake the same way, character for character. This is what either prints for the first example above, a reference kept across a push:

  • The first line says what went wrong. error means the program was rejected before it ran; a check that fails while the program runs is a fault instead (fault[diag.index-out-of-bounds]: index out of bounds), and the program stops there. In the brackets is the diagnostic's identifier: it is the same in every implementation and every version, and the specification's diagnostic registry has an entry for each.
  • --> gives the file, the line and the column, in the form editors and terminals turn into a link.
  • The source line, with carets under the token the rule applies to.
  • = repair: is the registry's advice for this diagnostic.

coby --explain tour.cb (or cobc --explain) adds the registry's whole entry: the rule of the specification that rejected the program, the invariant it protects, what it required and what it observed, and the examples that show it. A compiled program shows its faults that way when it runs with COBALTC_EXPLAIN=1 in its environment.

A line that begins internal error in coby: (or cobc:) is not about your program: it is a bug in the tool, which exits with status 4 and names the place in its own source. Please report it with the program that caused it; RUST_BACKTRACE=1 adds the tool's backtrace.

What you just saw

  • Declarations are type-first, like C: i32 x = 5;, Vec<Reading> entries;. auto infers the type from the initialiser. Function return types follow a colon: fn judge(…) : Verdict.
  • Blocks, if and match are expressions. The last expression in a block, with no semicolon, is the block's value. judge returns whatever branch of the if runs.
  • Conditions need parentheses (if (c), while (c), match (e)); match arms are Pattern : expression,, and a match must cover every variant (a missing one is rejected, above). A pattern can also be a condition: if (Some(n) = HashMap::get(…)) runs its block only when the lookup found something, with n bound.
  • &x is a shared (read-only) reference and &mut x an exclusive one. The compiler checks every use: a reference kept into the Vec across a push, a value used after it moved, are rejected before the program runs (above). &log.entries[0 .. 2] is a slice, a borrowed run of elements.
  • Log is a resource: it owns a Vec and a HashMap. Its destructor fn Log::drop runs at the end of main, then its fields are freed. Passing or assigning a resource moves it.
  • String, HashMap and sprintf. sprintf("sensor-%d", s) builds a String; *HashMap::entry(&mut m, key, 0) += 1 counts. The standard library lives in the module std, imported by import std;.
  • Errors are values. A Result must be used (dropping one is rejected), ? returns an Err or a None early, and checked_add turns an overflow into None. Plain arithmetic that overflows is never silent: it is rejected when the compiler can see it, and stops the program when it happens.
  • No implicit conversions. widen<i32>(b - b'0') and narrow<i32>(n) say what happens to the representation; narrow checks that the value fits.
  • Library calls are qualified: Vec::push(&mut v, x), Vec::sort(&mut v), HashMap::get(&m, &k). There is no method-call syntax.
  • Generics, closures and threads. larger<T: integer> works for any integer type; to_f is a closure whose capture list names what it uses; spawn starts a thread and join waits for its result. The two threads share their counter only through a mutex: lock is the only way in.

Further showcases can be found in the repository's showcase directory; its README describes them all.

Core language and std

Which parts of CobaltC are the language itself, always available, and which come from the standard library and need import std;.

CobaltC comes in two layers. The core language is always there: its types, its constructs, and a set of intrinsics, functions defined by a rule of the specification rather than by a body. The standard library, std, is a module, written mostly in CobaltC itself. Nothing of std is in scope until a module writes import std;, and each module imports it for itself (§17). This page says which layer each part belongs to.

Core: always available, no import

Types built into the language

  • Integers i8–i128, u8–u128, isize, usize; floats f32, f64
  • bool, str (string literals), void / ()
  • array<T, N>, slice<T, shared> and slice<T, exclusive>
  • ref<T, shared> and ref<T, exclusive>, rawptr<T>
  • fn(…) : R values and closures
  • handle<T> (a thread), mutex<T>, guard<T>

Language constructs

struct, bitstruct, enum (with numeric codes), resource, destructors (Type::drop), generics with the built-in bounds eq, ordered, number, integer and clone, match with nested, literal and text patterns, if and while (either with a pattern as the condition), for, foreach (over collections and ranges), break, continue, ?, const, modules and import, unsafe, unsafe extern fn and extern "code";.

allocate returns a Result, which a program can use without the import even though it cannot name the Result type without it.

Intrinsics private to std

key_hash, key_eq, key_less, key_less_at, swap_places, append_native, text_write, parse_check, parse_value, str_slice (beneath StringView::of), and the names that begin with $: the machinery std's own code is built on. A program cannot call them, nor std's private externs stderr_write, which eprintf writes through, and stdout_flush, beneath flush_stdout.

std: needs import std;

Mostly written in CobaltC itself; a few parts are provided natively by each implementation. std is divided into submodules by subject, and import std; brings in all of them, so a program never needs to know which holds what; the column says, for a program that wants one subject alone (import std::text;). §21 covers it in full.

What may surprise you

  • printf and assert are std, not core: a program without the import cannot print.
  • Vec, String and Option are std, but array, str, slice, handle and mutex are core.
  • swap, the one to use, is std; swap_places, which it is built on, is private to std.
  • min and max are std; min_value and max_value are core.
  • sqrt, round and the other floating-point functions are std (std::math), not core: they are ordinary library functions, so they need the import, and a function of your own named round is an ordinary name.
← A tour in one programTopCobaltC for C programmers →

CobaltC for C programmers

What carries over from C, what the same words mean here, the habits the compiler stops, and how error handling works in place of return codes, errno, NULL and abort.

If you write C, most of CobaltC will look familiar and a few things will look wrong. This section is the shortest path from one to the other: it says what you can keep doing, what the same spelling means here, which three habits the compiler will stop, and, at the greatest length, how a program reports and handles failure, because that is where C and CobaltC differ most and where the reference sections take the longest to connect. Everything here is said again, more fully, in the sections it links to; this is the map.

What carries over

Declarations are type-first, blocks are braces, statements end in ;, comments start with //, and printf is printf. if, while, for (init; cond; step), break, continue and return are what you expect, and &&, ||, !, the arithmetic, bitwise and comparison operators have C's spellings and precedences. A struct is a struct, written with C99's designated initialisers and nothing else: Point { .x = 3, .y = 4 }. main may return a u8, which is the process's exit status, and the program's arguments are arg_count() and arg(i).

Three small things in that program are not C. fn main() : u8 puts the return type after a colon, as every function does. import std; brings in the standard library, which is where printf lives; without it the name is unknown (Core language and std). And the last line of main is 0 with no return and no semicolon: a block's final expression is its value, so if, match and plain blocks are expressions too, which is how CobaltC does without the ?: operator. return 0; would also have been fine.

The same words, a different meaning

Two spellings deserve a warning because they parse and mean something else. ? after an expression is not the start of a conditional: it propagates an error and returns from the function (below). And &x always makes a reference the compiler tracks, never an address you can add to; the address is rawptr_of(&x), usable only in unsafe.

Three habits the compiler stops

Overflow is not silent. In C, unsigned arithmetic wraps and signed overflow is undefined. Here +, - and * are checked: a result that leaves the type faults the program with diag.arith-overflow, division by zero with diag.div-by-zero. When you want wrapping, say so with wrapping_add and friends; when you want to detect it, checked_add returns an Option (§06).

Nothing converts implicitly. int to long, char to int, float to double, a pointer to bool: none of it happens. Every change of representation is a named intrinsic, and the ones that can lose information check the value (§06, Conversions are explicit). The error message tells you which one to write.

Pointers do not escape. A reference to a local cannot be returned or stored anywhere that outlives the local; a reference into a Vec cannot be kept across a push that may move the elements; a value cannot be used after it was moved. These are rejected before the program runs where the compiler can see them (diag.reference-escapes-scope, diag.stale-binding) and stop the program at the first use otherwise (§09, §10). There is no dangling pointer to find later.

Memory: no malloc, no free

Every value has one owner, and when the owner's scope ends the value is destroyed, on every path out of the scope: a normal end, an early return, a ? that returns an error, or the unwinding of a fault. A Vec frees its buffer, a String its bytes, a File closes. Your own type joins in by being declared resource and giving fn T::drop, the destructor, which runs first; the fields follow. This replaces the cleanup: label, the matching free for each malloc, and the fclose someone forgot on one error path. Passing or assigning a resource moves it: the new name owns it, the old name is dead, and using the old name is an error. Plain values (numbers, bool, references, small structs of them) are copied as in C.

Library calls name the type they belong to and write the borrow they take: Vec::push(&mut v, x), Vec::len(&v). There is no v.push(x); the . is only field access. The mode of every access, & or &mut, is visible at the call (§08).

Strings

A string is bytes with a length, in UTF-8, with no terminating zero. A literal is a str: read-only, indexed by byte with str_byte(s, i), measured with str_len(s). Text you build or own is a String (String::from_str, String::append, sprintf); text you only look at, passed to a function, is a StringView (§21, Which text type?). Comparison is a function (String::eq_str, StringView::eq), never == on pointers, and %s prints any of the three.

Error handling, from the beginning

C has one mechanism for everything that can go wrong, and it is a convention: a function returns a value that means failure (-1, NULL, EOF, false), perhaps sets errno, and the caller checks, or does not. Bugs and expected failures travel the same road, nothing forces the check, and cleanup on the way out is the caller's problem. CobaltC separates the two kinds of failure and gives each its own mechanism, and that separation is the thing to learn first; the syntax follows from it.

An error valueA fault
What it isAn expected failure the program may recover from: bad input, a missing file, a full queue, a lookup that finds nothingA violated rule of the language: overflow, an index out of range, a dead reference, a failed assert, an unwrap of nothing
How it travelsAs a value: Result<T, E> or Option<T>, returned like any other valueIt does not: the thread unwinds every scope, running destructors, and the program ends with the fault's name and exit status 1
Who decidesThe caller, with match, ?, if (Some(x) = …), unwrap_orNobody: there is no catch (a spawned thread's fault can be contained at its join, §19)
In C termsthe return code, done so that it cannot be ignoredabort(), done so that it runs your cleanup first

The rule of thumb: if a failure is part of normal operation, it is an error value; if it can only happen because the program is wrong, let the fault fire and fix the program. Do not wrap arithmetic in Result, and do not assert that a file exists.

Option in place of NULL and sentinels

Option<T> is Some(v) or None. It is a plain two-variant enum from std, not a pointer, so a function that may have nothing to return says so in its type and the caller cannot forget to look: there is no way to use the T without taking the Option apart. There are four ways to take it apart, and C programmers tend to reach for the last one first.

The fourth way is Option::unwrap(o), or Option::expect(o, "why it must be there"): it gives the value or faults with diag.unwrap-failed. That is the right tool exactly when None would mean the program is wrong, as assert is; in a library function, or anywhere the caller could reasonably have passed nothing, it is the wrong one, because it turns the caller's input into your crash. If you find yourself writing if (Option::is_some(&o)) { … Option::unwrap(o) … }, write the if (Some(x) = o) form instead: it binds the value and checks in one step.

Result in place of return codes and errno

Result<T, E> is Ok(v) or Err(e). E is any type, and the idiom is an enum you declare for the module, one variant per way things fail, carrying what the caller needs to say something useful (Invalid(usize): at which position). Compared with an int and errno: the value and the failure are one object, so they cannot get out of step; the error carries data, not a number to look up; and a Result that is not looked at is rejected by the compiler (diag.result-discarded), so the one failure mode C cannot prevent, the ignored return code, does not compile. If you really mean to drop it, say so: _ = save(x);.

std's own functions follow the same shape. File::open is Result<File, FileError>; String::parse<u32> is Result<u32, ParseError>; HashMap::get is Option<ref<V, shared>>. Every std error enum has a text function that gives a short sentence for a message (FileError::text(&e)), which is what a program prints when it gives up (§21).

?: the early return, in one character

Most C error handling is the same four lines repeated: call, test the code, clean up, return the code to the caller. ? is those four lines. Written after an expression of type Result<T, E>, in a function whose own return type is Result<_, E>, it yields the T when the value is Ok and otherwise returns the Err from the enclosing function at once, running the destructors of everything in scope on the way, as any return does. Inside a function returning Option, ? does the same for None. Three things follow, and they are the three things that confuse newcomers:

  • The function must be able to return the error. ? on a Result<T, E> needs an enclosing return type of Result<_, E>, with the same E. In a function returning u8 or nothing, ? is rejected: diag.propagate-outside-fallible-context. So main, which returns u8 or nothing, cannot use ?; the pattern below deals with that.
  • Different error types do not mix on their own. A function that calls into two libraries with two error enums must convert each to its own: Result::map_err(r, f) applies f to the Err and leaves an Ok alone, and a closure [](ParseError e) : ConfigError { BadNumber(e) } is the usual f, wrapping the inner error in a variant of the outer. The conversion is explicit at each boundary, and that is where you decide what the caller is told.
  • Option and Result do not mix either. Option::ok_or(o, e) turns None into Err(e) so that ? can return it: u32 n = Option::ok_or(checked_add(a, b), TooLarge)?; reads "the sum, or report TooLarge". Result::ok(r) goes the other way, dropping the error.

The whole shape of a program

Put together, a CobaltC program that can fail has three layers, and the layering is what to copy. At the bottom, functions return Result with the module's error enum and use ? to pass failures up. In the middle, a function converts foreign errors into that enum with map_err and ok_or, so the layer above sees one type. At the top, main cannot use ? and should not try: it calls one function that does the work and returns a Result, matches once, prints the error's text to standard error and returns a non-zero status. That match is the only place in the program that decides how a failure is reported, which is where a C programmer expects perror and exit(1) to be.

Read port against the C version you would write: the if (!s[0]) return -1;, the strtoul with its endptr and errno check, the range test, each returning a different negative number the caller has to know. Here each failure is a named variant, the parse error from std is kept inside BadNumber rather than flattened to a code, and run has no error handling at all: two ? and the happy path. The exit status is 1 and the message is on standard error, so the program behaves as a shell expects, and the output above shows only what reached standard output before the second port failed.

Reading the ? error
? is not a switch default and not the ternary operator; it is return Err(e) with the cleanup done for you. When it is rejected, the message says the function cannot return the error: either give the function a Result return type and let the caller decide, or handle the value here with match.

Faults: what abort() should have been

A fault is the language refusing to continue: an overflow, an index out of range, a division by zero, an unwrap of None, a false assert, a reference used after its referent ended. Nothing in the program can catch it, which is the point: the code after the failed check would have run on a state the check protected. What a fault does do, unlike abort(), is unwind. The faulting thread leaves every open scope in order, running every destructor, so files are closed and locks released, and only then does the program end, printing the fault's name, its location and the source line, with exit status 1.

assert is the one fault you raise yourself. Unlike C's, it is never compiled out, so it is a statement about the program that holds in every build; and its message is a printf format whose arguments are evaluated only when the condition is false, so a precise message costs nothing while things are right.

Whether something should be an assert or an Err is the same question as before: can a correct program, given legitimate input, reach it? An empty Vec passed to average by a caller who read it from a file can, so in a real program average would return Option<i32>; the assert is right only if the caller has already guaranteed the length. When a fault happens in a thread you spawned, it ends that thread alone and becomes the thread's result, which join raises and try_join hands over as a value (§19, When a thread fails); the main thread's fault always ends the program.

The idioms, side by side

CCobaltC
if (p == NULL) return -1;? on an Option in a function returning Option; or Option::ok_or(o, MyError)? in one returning Result
if (rc < 0) { cleanup(); return rc; }T v = call()?; with the module's error type; destructors do the cleanup
if (rc < 0) { cleanup(); return MY_ERR; }Result::map_err(call(), [](TheirError e) : MyError { Wrapped(e) })?
switch (rc) { case E_A: … case E_B: … }match (e) { A : …, B(detail) : …, }, every variant covered
perror("open"); exit(1);in main: Err(e) : { eprintf("open: %s\n", FileError::text(&e)); 1 }
x = f(); /* ignore */_ = f();, the only way to drop a Result
assert(n > 0);assert(n > 0, "n was %d", n);
abort(), exit(EXIT_FAILURE)exit(1), after unwinding; or return 1 from fn main() : u8
a flag ok threaded through a loopwhile (Some(item) = next(&mut it)) { … } or foreach, with ? inside a Result-returning function
errno read after the callthe payload of the Err variant, or E::text(&e) for a sentence

Building and calling C

There is no header, no object file to manage and no Makefile. cobc prog.cb compiles the program and the files it names with module m "./m.cb";, then links; coby prog.cb runs it directly; cobc --check prog.cb only checks. Calling C is a declaration and a file: unsafe extern fn area(i32 w, i32 h) : i32; promises the signature, extern "./shapes.c"; names the source (or extern "m"; a library), and every call sits in an unsafe block, because the compiler cannot see what the C does (§20). The types at the boundary are the C-compatible ones: sized integers, floats, bool, rawptr<T>. Everything you have written in C stays callable; what changes is that the boundary is marked, and the safe side of it keeps every guarantee of this section.

Rules of thumb
  • Reach for Option where you reached for NULL or -1, for Result where you reached for a return code, and for a fault (assert) only where the program would be wrong.
  • Give each module one error enum, convert foreign errors into it with map_err and ok_or at the boundary, and use ? everywhere else.
  • Let main match once: print E::text(&e) to standard error and return a non-zero u8.
  • Trust the destructors: there is no cleanup label to jump to, because every path out of a scope runs them.
← Core language and stdTopCobaltC and Rust →

CobaltC and Rust

What the two languages share, where they part company, and the price and payoff of each choice: when a check happens, what a type says, generics, threads, failure, unsafe and the surface.

Rust and CobaltC want the same things: no null, no dangling reference, no data race, no use after free, one owner per resource, every failure a value or a named stop, and all of it without a garbage collector or a hidden runtime. A Rust programmer will recognise most of CobaltC on sight, which makes the places where the two part company the interesting ones. This section goes through them: when a check happens, what a type says, how generic code is written, how threads share, how failure is reported, what unsafe means, and what the surface looks like. It takes no side. Each choice has a price and a payoff, and the point is to say what they are. Rust is a mature language with a large ecosystem; CobaltC is a small one with a complete written semantics and two implementations that share it. Which matters more depends on what you are doing.

What the two share

  • Ownership and moves. A resource has one owner; assigning or passing it moves it, and the old name is unusable afterwards. In Rust every non-Copy type moves; in CobaltC a type is either plain (copied) or a resource (moved), decided by its declaration: struct or resource struct, and anything that holds a resource.
  • Shared or exclusive access, never both. Rust's &T and &mut T are CobaltC's ref<T, shared> and ref<T, exclusive>, written &x and &mut x in both. Any number of readers, or one writer, to one object at a time.
  • Destruction at scope end. Rust's Drop is CobaltC's Type::drop; both run in reverse order of declaration, on every path out, including a panic or a fault.
  • Option, Result and ?. The same two types, the same operator, the same habit of making absence and failure part of a function's type. Neither has exceptions.
  • Enums with payloads and exhaustive match. A closed set of alternatives, each carrying data, taken apart by patterns the compiler checks for completeness.
  • Generics compiled per use. Both monomorphise: a generic function becomes one copy per set of concrete types, with no run-time type information.
  • Explicit conversions. Neither converts numeric types silently. Rust writes as and From; CobaltC writes widen, narrow and reinterpret.
  • A marked boundary. Raw pointers and foreign functions live inside unsafe in both, and both say that safe code cannot break the language's guarantees.

When a check happens

This is the difference everything else follows from. Whether a reference is used after its object has gone, or while another part of the program writes through a second reference, depends on what the program does when it runs; no checker can decide it exactly for every program. Each language turns that into a question it can answer, and they turn it in opposite directions.

Rust decides at compile time, by over-approximating. Every reference type carries a lifetime, an upper bound on how long the reference may be used, written as 'a or filled in by three elision rules. Every function signature states how its result's lifetime relates to its parameters'. The borrow checker then checks each function body against its own signature, one function at a time, following the flow of the code to see which borrows are live where. Nothing is checked at run time, and nothing is paid at run time. The price is that the checker must be conservative: when it cannot prove a program safe, it rejects it, correct or not, and the programmer restructures, adds annotations, or steps into unsafe. Two exclusive references into one vector at indices known only at run time, a struct that refers into itself, a reference kept across a call that might reallocate: all rejected, because the proof is not in the text.

CobaltC decides at run time, against the actual state. A reference carries no lifetime; its validity is a fact about the running program: which object it reaches, whether that object still exists, which other references to it are live and in what mode. The language's rules are written over that state, and the interpreter and the compiled program check them at each access. The price is a run-time cost and a fault instead of a compile error: a mistake becomes a named diagnostic at the step that commits it, in the run that reaches it, and a path no test runs is a path no check has run. The payoff is that no annotation is needed and no correct program is refused for lack of a proof. Both languages are in fact hybrids. Rust keeps run-time checks for the cases its static rule cannot express (RefCell, Mutex, Rc, bounds, and overflow in debug builds); CobaltC rejects at compile time what its checker can see without running the program (§10, §14). The difference is the default, and what each asks of the programmer where the default fails.

Rust refuses that program: with i and j unknown, it cannot prove the two borrows disjoint, so the programmer writes split_at_mut or indexes twice. CobaltC accepts it and checks the indices as the borrows are made. Run it with j = 1 and the second borrow is the fault diag.aliasing-conflict, at that line, in that run. Rust's answer is the same in both cases and arrives before the program exists; CobaltC's is different in the two cases and arrives when it runs.

In Rust, Holder would be Holder<'a>, keep would carry the same 'a, and the second assignment would not compile, because h outlives inner. CobaltC has no 'a to carry, so the escape through keep is invisible to the checker and the program runs until the read, which faults. The same escape written in one function, with no call between, is caught before the program runs, because there the checker can see it:

Moving or destroying a value while a reference to it is live, and writing to a vector while a reference into it is live, are likewise compile-time errors in both languages when the two uses are in one function (§08, §10); Rust also catches them across functions, through signatures; CobaltC catches those at run time.

What a type says

Because Rust's checks are static, its types must carry what the checker needs; because CobaltC's are dynamic, its types carry less and its run-time state carries the rest. That shows up in four places.

RustCobaltC
A reference&'a T, &'a mut T: a lifetime (usually elided) bounds every useref<T, shared>, ref<T, exclusive>: no lifetime; validity is checked at each use (§09)
A struct holding a referencestruct Holder<'a> { r: &'a i32 }: the lifetime is a parameter of the typestruct Holder { ref<i32, shared> r; }: the reference is tied to the storage holding it and the object it reaches, at run time (§10)
A function returning a referencethe result's lifetime is related to a parameter's by elision or by writing 'a; any relation can be statedelided when exactly one parameter is a reference; with two or more, returning a reference is refused outright (diag.lifetime-elision-ambiguous): return a copy, an index or an owned value instead
What may cross to another threadSend and Sync marker traits, checked at compile time; spawn wants 'static data, scoped threads borrowany value moves; a reference may be lent for the thread's life and is checked at run time (§19)

Rust lets longest be written by naming the relation; CobaltC, having no names for lifetimes (that choice is final, D-0011 and CHG-0022), refuses the shape and asks for a function that returns which one, or a copy. In exchange, a CobaltC signature never needs a lifetime, and a reference stored in a Vec, a HashMap or a closure needs no type parameter to say how long it lives.

Generics: traits against bounds

Rust's generics are organised by traits: a type implements a trait, a generic function requires one (T: Ord), and traits also serve as interfaces, as operator overloading, as the mechanism for iteration, formatting, conversion, and, through dyn Trait, as run-time polymorphism. Most of Rust's expressiveness and most of its learning curve are there. CobaltC has no traits. A generic parameter takes one of five built-in bounds, ordered, number, integer, clone or plain, which name what the language itself knows about a type (§12); a type joins clone by defining T::clone, and nothing else is user-extensible. There is no operator overloading, no interface a user type can implement, and no run-time dispatch except through function values and closures. Where a Rust program would define a trait and implement it for several types, a CobaltC program writes an enum of those types and a match, or passes the behaviour as a function value. That is a real limit on what can be abstracted over, chosen so that a call always names the function it calls (§15).

Neither language has inheritance. Both monomorphise, so generic code costs nothing at run time in either. Rust infers types across a whole function, forwards and backwards; CobaltC's inference flows downward only, from a declaration or an expected type into an expression, which is why its variables are usually declared with a type and auto is the exception.

Mutability

Rust marks the binding: let x is immutable, let mut x may be assigned and borrowed exclusively, and a &mut can only be taken from a mut binding. CobaltC marks nothing on a variable: any variable may be assigned, and the question is only ever about references, which are shared or exclusive (§08). What Rust's mut buys is documentation and a compile-time refusal to change what was declared unchanging; what CobaltC's absence of it buys is one fewer word on every declaration and no second meaning for mut. Both make a const a compile-time constant only.

Integers

Both have the same sized integer types and the same wrapping_, saturating_ and checked_ operations. They differ on what plain + does when it overflows. In Rust it panics in a debug build and wraps in a release build unless overflow checks are turned on; a shipped program usually wraps. In CobaltC it is a fault, always, in both the interpreter and the compiled program (§06): there is no build in which an overflow is silent. The compiled cost of that choice is measurable and modest (P): on the repository's benchmarks a CobaltC program compiled through C runs between about the same time as the Rust program and about twice it, and much of the gap is the arithmetic checks that a Rust release build leaves out.

Threads

Rust makes a data race a type error: a value crosses to another thread only if it is Send, is shared only if it is Sync, and spawn requires what it captures to live for the whole program, so sharing goes through Arc<Mutex<T>> or a scoped thread whose borrows the checker can see end. CobaltC's spawn moves its arguments or lends a reference for the thread's life, and the check that two threads never touch one object incompatibly is the same run-time alias check as within one thread; a mutex guard, an Atomic, a Channel or an Arc are the ways to share on purpose (§19). What that gives CobaltC, and Rust does not set out to give, is an account of every schedule: a program's threads interleave at the granularity of single operations under rules the specification states, so --explore can run a program under many schedules and report every distinct outcome, and a wait that no thread can end is a diagnostic, diag.deadlock, rather than a hang. Rust has no equivalent in the language; it has tools outside it. Both unwind a failed thread and hand the failure to whoever joins it; both poison a mutex the failed thread held. CobaltC has no condition variables and no memory orderings weaker than sequential consistency; Rust has both.

Failure

Both languages separate expected failure, a Result or an Option the caller handles, from a bug, which stops the program. Rust's stop is a panic: it unwinds the thread, running destructors, can be caught with catch_unwind, and in a release build an overflow or an out-of-bounds index may be a panic or, for overflow, nothing at all. CobaltC's stop is a fault: every fault has a name in a registry (the appendix) and a location, it unwinds running destructors, it is the same in the interpreter and the compiled program, and it is contained only at the two boundaries the language names, a supervised thread and a C-callable library entry (§18). Rust's error enums are usually hand-written or generated by a library; CobaltC's are hand-written, with map_err and ok_or at the edges. ? means the same thing.

Unsafe

In both, unsafe marks where the programmer, not the language, vouches for a claim. In Rust the claims are about the absence of undefined behaviour: a raw pointer is valid, aliasing rules are respected, a foreign function's contract holds; a wrong claim is undefined behaviour, and the rules for what unsafe code may assume are still being settled (Stacked Borrows, Tree Borrows). In CobaltC the claims are stated as side-conditions of named trusted rules (§20): a raw read or write, a reclaim of raw memory, a call across the boundary, each with what it asserts. The standard library's own unsafe blocks are listed with their claims. The interpreter simulates raw memory and checks even trusted operations against it, so a wrong claim is a fault there; the compiled program trusts the claim, as Rust does. Both languages hold that safe code cannot break the invariants; neither can promise anything once a trusted claim is false.

The surface

RustCobaltC
Declarationslet x: T = …;, let mutT x = …;, auto x = …;; no mut
Functionsfn f(x: T) -> U { … }fn f(T x) : U { … }
Methodsimpl T { fn m(&self) }, called x.m()fn T::m(ref<T, shared> x), called T::m(&x); there is no method-call syntax, by decision (§22)
Patternsmatch v { Some(x) => …, None => … }match (v) { Some(x) : …, None : …, }
Closures|x| x + k, captures inferred[k](i32 x) : i32 { x + k }, captures listed (§15)
Loopsloop, while, for x in iterwhile, for (init; cond; step), foreach (x in &v)
Text&str, Stringstr, String, StringView (§21)
Conversionsx as T, T::from(x), x.into()widen<T>(x), narrow<T>(x), reinterpret<T>(x); as is reserved
Formattingprintln!("{x} {y:?}"), a macroprintf("%v %v\\n", x, y), a built-in whose format is checked
Modulesmod, use, crates, pubmodule, import, export; one standard library, no package manager (§17)
Macrosdeclarative and proceduralnone
Traitstrait, impl … for, dynfive built-in bounds; T::clone and T::drop by name

Semantics and tooling

Rust's meaning is given by its reference, its compiler and its test suite, with a formal specification (Ferrocene) written after the fact and a model of unsafe code still in research. It has one compiler, cargo, crates.io, rustdoc, rust-analyzer, clippy and Miri, a stable release since 2015, and targets from microcontrollers to every major operating system. CobaltC's meaning is its specification, written as rules before either implementation; the interpreter runs those rules and the compiler must match it byte for byte on every conformance case, every showcase and every example in this guide; a model checker enumerates the small programs' outcomes. It has an interpreter, a compiler through C, a formatter, a standard library with no third-party code, and two targets, x86-64 Linux and Windows. One is a production language with an ecosystem; the other is a language whose whole behaviour can be read, run and argued about.

The trade, in one place
Neither approach is free. A static guarantee is paid for in annotations and in programs refused for want of a proof; a dynamic one is paid for at run time and in bugs found by running rather than by compiling. Rust puts the proof in the types and makes the exceptions dynamic; CobaltC puts the check in the run and makes the obvious cases static. Which is right depends on whether the cost of a check at run time or the cost of a proof at compile time is the one you can afford, and on whether you need a language's behaviour to be fully stated or its ecosystem to be fully grown.
← CobaltC for C programmersTop§06 Arithmetic and numeric types →

§06Arithmetic and numeric types

Governing specification file: spec/06-arithmetic.md

Checked integer arithmetic, explicit conversions, how literals get their types, and the sizes and limits of types.

Numbers are where silent corruption usually starts, so CobaltC's arithmetic is checked by default: an operation whose mathematical result does not fit its type does not wrap around, it faults. Every other policy (wrapping, saturating, or returning None) is a named function you call on purpose. Types never convert implicitly; every change of representation is a named intrinsic with a documented behaviour.

Numeric types

TypeMeaningNotes
i8 i16 i32 i64 i128signed integers of the given widthtwo's complement
u8 u16 u32 u64 u128unsigned integers of the given width
isize usizesigned / unsigned integers of address widththe types of indices, lengths, sizes and pointer offsets; the width (16, 32, 64 or 128 bits) is fixed and documented by each implementation
f32 f64IEEE 754 binary32 / binary64±Inf and NaN are ordinary values; float arithmetic never faults
booltrue or falseproduced by comparisons and && || !

There is no implicit promotion: i32 + i64 is a type error, and a u8 cannot be passed where an i32 is expected. Unary minus applies only to signed and float types.

Literals

Integer literals are digit strings: decimal, or hexadecimal, octal or binary after 0x, 0o or 0b (0xFF, 0o755, 0b1010), with no sign. A _ between two digits groups them and is ignored: 1_000_000, 0xFFFF_0000, 3.141_592 (anywhere else, a _ is a syntax error). A literal's type comes from, in order: an explicit suffix 123: u8; the expected type at that position (a declared variable type, a parameter type, a field type, or the other operand of the same operator); otherwise the default, i32 for integers and f64 for floats. An expression made only of literals and operators takes the expected type as a whole, so u64 x = 1024 * 1024 * 1024 * 16; is computed in u64, while auto y = 65536 * 65536; has no expected type, is an i32, and overflows. A literal that does not fit its type is a static error. A minus written directly before an integer literal is checked with it, as one negative value, so -2147483648 is the smallest i32. A type's limits also have names, min_value<i32>() and max_value<i32>() (below). Float literals are digits . digits, with an optional exponent (1.5e-3, 2.5E3, or 1e5 with no fraction), optionally suffixed : f32; one too large for its type (1e400) is a static error, not infinity. A byte character b'a' is one ASCII character or an escape (b'\n', b'\'', b'\x7f'), for writing bytes readably in code that parses. It is a number like any other literal and takes an unsigned type from its context (u32 c = …; c == b'|' compares two u32s), and is a u8 when nothing fixes its type; a signed context is a type error. A string literal "…" is always a str and a byte literal b"…" always an array<u8, N> (§21, §22); neither takes an expected type.

Checked arithmetic

+, - and * on integers fault with diag.arith-overflow when the result leaves the type's range. / and % truncate toward zero (the remainder takes the sign of the dividend); dividing by zero is diag.div-by-zero, and the one overflowing division, the minimum value of a signed type divided by -1, is diag.div-overflow. Negating the minimum signed value is an overflow too. When both operands are literals the fault is detected statically and the program is rejected; otherwise it is a run-time fault that terminates the program (see §18). A local initialized with a literal counts as that literal until something writes it, borrows it or captures it in a closure, so u8 x = 200; u8 y = x + 100; is rejected too. After such a write, or after an if that writes it on only one branch, the check happens at run time.

Choosing a different overflow policy

When wrapping or clamping is what you actually want, say so. The wrapping_ and saturating_ families never fault; the checked_ family returns an Option so the caller can decide. These are ordinary generic calls with the operand type inferred from the arguments.

CallResultOn overflow
wrapping_add(a, b), wrapping_sub, wrapping_mulsame typewraps modulo 2N
saturating_add(a, b), saturating_sub, saturating_mulsame typeclamps to the type's minimum or maximum
checked_add(a, b), checked_sub, checked_mul, checked_div, checked_remOption<T>None (also for division by zero)
checked_neg(a)Option<T>None for the most negative value, and for any non-zero unsigned value

Shifts, bitwise operators and comparison

  • << and >> take a u32 shift amount that must be less than the type's bit width; anything else is diag.shift-amount-out-of-range. Left shift discards high bits by definition (it is not an overflow); right shift is arithmetic on signed types.
  • &, |, ^ and ~ work on any integer type; ! is boolean not.
  • == != < <= > >= compare two operands of the same type and yield bool. Floats follow IEEE rules: every comparison involving NaN is false except !=.

Conversions are explicit

There is exactly one way to change a number's type: call the intrinsic that names the conversion. Each takes the target type as a type argument.

Five intrinsics work on an integer's bits directly: count_ones(x), leading_zeros(x) and trailing_zeros(x) (each a u32; zero gives the type's width), and rotate_left(x, k) and rotate_right(x, k) (by k modulo the width, keeping x's type). They act on the value's cell image, so a negative i8 has eight ones, and none of them faults (D-0123).

IntrinsicFrom → toBehaviour
widen<U>(x)integer to a wider integer whose range contains every value; f32 to f64always exact, never faults (u8 → i32, i32 → i64, f32 → f64)
narrow<U>(x)any integer to any integerchecked: diag.narrowing-overflow if x does not fit
checked_narrow<T>(x)any integer to any integerOption<T>: Some(x) when x fits T, else None — for a value from outside, where a fault would be wrong (D-0122)
narrow_wrapping<U>(x)any integer to any integerkeeps the low bits, never faults
reinterpret<U>(x)between the signed and unsigned types of one width (and usize ⇄ isize); between a float and an integer of its width (f32 ⇄ u32/i32, f64 ⇄ u64/i64)the same bit pattern read as the other type
to_float<U>(x)any integer or float to f32/f64nearest representable value (ties to even); beyond the target's range an infinity, as float arithmetic gives; NaN stays NaN
to_int<U>(x)float to integertruncates toward zero; checked: infinities, NaN and out-of-range values fault

Between the two float types: widen<f64>(x) takes an f32 to an f64 exactly, and to_float<f32>(x) takes an f64 to the nearest f32, rounding as float arithmetic does. There is no widen<f32> of an f64, since most f64 values have no exact f32. reinterpret gives a float's IEEE-754 bits as an integer of the same width, and turns such an integer back into a float, with no unsafe.

widen is only accepted where every value of the source fits the target, so it can never lose one: widen<u64> of an i32 is a static error, because a negative i32 has no u64 value. narrow works between any two integer types, and never faults where the value fits. Use it for usize and isize: whether usize → u64 is a widening depends on the address width, so narrow<u64>(n) is the spelling that is accepted by every implementation.

Sizes and limits of types

Four intrinsics describe a type rather than a value. Each takes the type as its type argument, written explicitly, and no other arguments.

IntrinsicResultMeaningFor
sizeof<T>()usizethe bytes a T occupies, padding includedany type
alignof<T>()usizethe alignment a T's address must have, in bytesany type
min_value<T>()Tthe smallest value of T (for a float, the most negative finite one)integer and float types
max_value<T>()Tthe largest value of T (for a float, the largest finite one)integer and float types

Every fixed-width type has the same size and limits on every implementation: sizeof<i32>() is 4 and max_value<i32>() is 2147483647. isize and usize have the address width, which each implementation documents, so for them the intrinsics are the portable way to write a size or limit, where a literal is not. A struct's size and alignment follow from its fields (§16): each field is aligned, and the struct's alignment is its largest field's.

Limits are most often the starting value of a search, a bound to clamp against, or a value that means "none". Here are all three:

A generic function may use the limits of its own type parameter. It cannot do arithmetic on a T without a bound (§12), but it can produce a T's limit and pass it on. Each use is checked when the function is instantiated, so a T that is not an integer type is rejected before the program runs.

Rules of thumb
  • Default arithmetic is checked. If you want wrapping, write wrapping_add; if you want to handle overflow, write checked_add and match on the Option.
  • Never expect a conversion to happen for you. Reach for widen first; use narrow (checked) or narrow_wrapping (deliberate truncation) when going the other way.
  • Use usize for lengths and indices, isize for pointer offsets, and suffix a literal (5: u8) when the context does not already fix its type.
  • Floats never fault. Remember that NaN is unequal to itself.
  • Write a type's limits as min_value<T>() and max_value<T>(). For isize and usize they are the only portable spelling.
← CobaltC and RustTop§07 Resources, ownership and destruction →

§07Resources, ownership and destruction

Governing specification file: spec/07-resource-authority.md

Resource types have exactly one owner, move instead of copying, and are destroyed automatically and exactly once.

Some values are just data: an i32, a bool, a struct of numbers. Copying them is harmless. Other values own something that must be released exactly once: a heap buffer, a file handle, a lock, a thread. CobaltC calls the second kind resources, and the rules in this section exist so that a resource always has exactly one owner, is never copied, and is destroyed exactly once, at a predictable moment, whether or not you remember to do it.

Plain types and resource types

A type is a resource if it is declared with the resource keyword, or if any of its fields, elements or payloads is a resource. Vec<T>, String, Rc<T>, a thread handle, a mutex and a lock guard are all resources. Numbers, bool, references, raw pointers and function values are plain. A struct of plain fields is plain; a struct containing a Vec is a resource by derivation, with no keyword needed.

One owner: moves, not copies

A resource lives in exactly one place. When you initialise a variable from it, pass it by value to a function, store it in a field, or return it, the resource moves: the new place becomes the owner and the old name becomes stale. Using a stale name is an error (diag.stale-binding), caught at compile time when the move is visible in the same function and at run time otherwise. A name moved on only some paths (in one branch of an if, or in a loop body that runs again) counts as moved: give it a new value on every path before using it again. Nothing is ever copied silently, so there can never be two owners.

Because a resource is never copied, it cannot appear where a copy would be made: you cannot compare two Vecs with ==, and you cannot read one out of a field of a live struct. Take a reference instead (§09), or move the whole container.

Automatic destruction

Every resource is destroyed automatically: a named resource when the block that declared it ends, and a temporary (an unnamed call result or literal) at the end of the statement that created it. Locals are destroyed in reverse order of creation. A struct's resource fields are destroyed after the struct's own destructor, innermost first, in reverse declaration order. A return, break, continue or run-time fault unwinds the same way. There is no way to leak a resource, so there is no leak diagnostic.

You can also destroy a resource early with drop(x). Afterwards x is stale until you give it a new value: once x's value has gone, moved away or dropped, x = e gives it a new one, which is destroyed at the end of x's own block like its first value. A value whose end only frees memory (a String, a Vec, a HashMap, an Option or struct made of such: a *quiet* type, D-0194) is simply replaced: s = String::from_str("new"); destroys the old String there. Assigning over any other resource that is still there is an error (diag.overwrite-of-live-resource), because its end does something you should see: a destructor of yours runs, a file closes, a thread is joined. Write overwrite(&mut x, e), which destroys the old value and stores the new one, or drop it first. The same holds for a field (g.file = f;) and for a write through a reference (*r = v;, r.rows = v;): where the compiler can see the old value is still there, it rejects the assignment before the program runs; elsewhere, the run does. What counts is whether the value there owns anything: a None of an Option<File> owns nothing, so o = Some(f); over it is fine, while a Some must be dropped first. A type declared resource, or with a destructor, always owns. Declaring the name again in the same block does not: that is diag.duplicate-local (§11).

Destructors

A type gets a destructor by declaring an associated function named drop that takes an exclusive reference to the value and returns nothing. The language calls it exactly once, when the resource is destroyed; you may not call it yourself. Inside it you can mutate the value but not move out of it. Field resources are destroyed after the body runs. The type must be a resource: declare it resource struct. A plain struct is copied and never destroyed, so a destructor on one would never run, and is refused (diag.destructor-on-plain-type).

Note
