Destructors run in reverse declaration order, last declared first, and a struct's fields in reverse field order, so what was built last is torn down first. The output above is a newline followed by 4321.

Things the rules forbid

The fix is overwrite(&mut l, Lock { .id = 2 });, which destroys the old Lock there (and prints its release where you wrote it), or drop(l); first. Two more rejections you will meet: drop(v) twice is diag.stale-binding (the first drop ended v); and moving a resource out of a field of a live struct (auto inner = holder.field;) is diag.move-out-of-field, because the struct would be left half-owned. Move the whole struct, or take a reference to the field.

Rules of thumb
  • If a type owns something, it is a resource: mark it resource and give it a drop. Types that merely contain resources become resources automatically.
  • Passing a resource by value hands it over. To let a callee look without taking, pass &x; to let it modify, pass &mut x.
  • Do not fight scope-end destruction. Put a resource in the smallest block that needs it and let the block end release it.
  • drop(x) is for early release. After it, x is gone until you give it a new value (x = e) or declare the name again.
← §06 Arithmetic and numeric typesTop§08 Aliasing: shared and exclusive access →

§08Aliasing: shared and exclusive access

Governing specification file: spec/08-alias-validity.md

Any number of readers, or one writer, never both. The rule is checked at every access, so a conflict cannot go unnoticed.

Two pieces of code touching one object at the same time is the root of most memory bugs: an iterator invalidated by a push, a struct half-updated by two threads, a buffer freed while something still points into it. CobaltC's answer is a discipline on access paths: every way of reaching an object (its name, a reference, a field projection) has a mode, and the modes that may coexist are fixed.

Two modes

ModeWrittenMayCoexists with
shared&x, type ref<T, shared>readany number of other shared paths
exclusive&mut x, type ref<T, exclusive>read and write; and, for the owner, move or destroynothing else that overlaps

A variable's own name is always an exclusive path: there is no mut keyword on bindings, because whether you may write is decided by what references currently exist, not by how the variable was declared. Restricting access is what a borrow does.

The one rule

At every read and every write, the language checks: is there another live path to the same storage whose mode conflicts with this access? Shared and shared never conflict. Anything involving an exclusive path conflicts, unless the other path is an ancestor of this one (the thing it was borrowed from). Forming a conflicting borrow is reported at once as diag.aliasing-conflict; so is using the owner while a conflicting borrow lives.

Borrows in one argument list are all formed before the call holds any of them, so passing two conflicting references to the same storage is accepted at the call. The conflict is reported at the first access inside the function that meets both, the point where it actually matters.

Most conflicts are reported before the program runs, marked (static): whenever the function body itself shows that a conflicting reference is certainly live. That covers a borrow held in a variable, a reborrow through a reference or a guard (&*r, &r.f), the binder of a match (&e) arm, and the arguments a thread was spawned with, until join. What one body cannot see, like the call above, is reported when the conflicting access runs, marked (dynamic).

When does a borrow end?

A reference lives as long as something holds it. A reference passed straight to a call dies when the statement ends, which is why consecutive calls that each borrow the same variable are fine. A reference, slice or StringView kept in a local variable lives until the last statement of its block that uses it, and ends there. So does any other local that holds references but owns nothing to destroy: the Option<ref<V, shared>> that HashMap::get returns, or a struct of references. Using it inside a loop, a branch or a nested block counts as a use by that whole statement, so a reference used in a loop lives through the loop. A reference variable lives to the end of its block, as before, when a closure captures it, when another reference was borrowed through it, or when a variable that can hold references (a Vec<StringView>, say) shares a statement with it and is used later, since that variable may keep a reference derived from it. A reference to data that holds no references (a ref<Vec<i32>, exclusive> parameter, a StringView) cannot keep one, so it counts only in a statement that could rebind it: one that assigns it, borrows it with &mut, or captures it in a closure.

A block ends every borrow it holds, so wrapping a borrow in a block still works, and reads well when a borrow should visibly end.

Reborrowing and ancestors

A path derived from another (a reborrow &*r, or a field projection r.a) has that path as its ancestor. Ancestors never conflict with their descendants, but the ancestor cannot be used in a conflicting way while a descendant lives. Once the descendants are gone, the ancestor is usable again.

Disjoint fields

Conflicts are decided by overlap of storage, not by which variable the paths come from. Two exclusive borrows of different fields of the same struct do not overlap and may coexist.

The write to p.b above is rejected because rb, a live exclusive path to exactly that storage, still exists until the block ends. The same applies to reading p.b through the owner: an exclusive child excludes every non-ancestor access, reads included, until it is gone. Confine the borrows to a block and the owner is free again:

Shared means read-only, all the way down

An exclusive path can only be derived from an exclusive path. Given a ref<T, shared> you cannot write through it and cannot reborrow it exclusively: the mode is part of the reference's type, so a function's signature tells the caller exactly what it may do. The other direction is always allowed: an exclusive reference can be passed to a function that asks for a shared one, and the function gets a shared reborrow of it (as if you had written &*r). With v : ref<Vec<T>, exclusive>, Vec::len(v) just works; likewise a slice<T, exclusive> for a slice<T, shared>.

All the way down includes the references a value holds. Read through a ref<S, shared>, an exclusive reference stored in S comes out as a shared one: you can read through it, keep it, pass it or return it as a ref<T, shared>, but not write through it. A copy of a value that holds an exclusive reference cannot be taken out through a shared reference either, and clone cannot copy one (diag.borrow-exceeds-source). A fn field is checked when it is called: a closure that writes a variable it captured cannot be called through a shared reference to the struct that holds it (diag.borrow-exceeds-source, at run time, since a fn type does not show what the closure captured). To change something through a value others share, put it in a mutex (§19).

Moving or destroying needs solitude

Moving a resource, or destroying it (with drop or at scope end), requires that no other path to it exists at all. Otherwise a reference would be left pointing at nothing.

Rules of thumb
  • Borrow shared (&x) by default; borrow exclusively (&mut x) only for the duration of the change.
  • Keep references short-lived. Passing &mut v directly as an argument creates a borrow that ends at the semicolon.
  • If the checker complains about a conflict, end the earlier borrow: put it in its own block, or reorder the code so the write happens after the last use of the reference.
  • Field-level borrows are precise: borrowing p.a exclusively leaves p.b free.
← §07 Resources, ownership and destructionTop§09 References →

§09References

Governing specification file: spec/09-identity-origin-extent.md

References are copyable values that name a place; dereferencing gives you that place back with every check intact.

A reference is the value form of an access path: a way to reach an object without owning it. References are plain values (copyable, no destroy authority) and carry their mode in their type. Raw pointers are a different thing entirely and live in §20.

Forming and using references

SyntaxMeaning
&ea ref<T, shared> to the place e
&mut ea ref<T, exclusive> to the place e
*rthe place r refers to: read it in an expression, assign to it, borrow it again, or project a field or element
r.f, r[i]field access and indexing look through a reference automatically
r1 == r2identity: true only if both refer to the same storage of the same object

The operand of & must be a place: a variable, a field, an element, or *r. You cannot borrow a temporary such as a call result or a literal (&make()); bind it to a variable first. This is rejected rather than given a lifetime because the temporary would end at the semicolon and take the reference with it.

The one place a temporary may be borrowed is as an argument: f(&make()) or printf("%v", &sprintf(…)). The value lives until the end of the statement, and the call is over before then. This works when the call's own result is not a reference, since such a result could carry the borrow out. An operator's result, the value ? gives, and a number or bool literal may be borrowed there too: HashMap::get(&m, &(k + 1)), Vec::len(&names()?), HashMap::get(&m, &3). A literal takes the type the parameter refers to, so &3 passed where a ref<u64, shared> is expected is a reference to a u64.

Part of a temporary may be borrowed there too: a field (String::len(&person().name)), an element, or a slice of an array literal or a call's result (sum(&[1, 2, 3][0..2])). A String that a call returns may be viewed the same way, so a computed path needs no binding: read_file(&sprintf("%s/%s", dir, name)[0..$]). It lives as long as the temporary does, to the end of the statement. A field can also be moved out of a temporary, String n = person().name;: the rest of the temporary ends at once, as if the struct had been destructured. That needs a struct without a destructor of its own.

References inside structs

A reference may be stored in a field. It then lives as long as the struct that holds it, which in turn may not outlive the referent (§10).

References as parameters

Passing &x or &mut x to a function creates a borrow that the parameter holds for the duration of the call and releases when the call returns. Inside the function the parameter is an ordinary reference. A parameter of type ref<T, exclusive> can be passed on to another call directly, without a new &mut, because it already is an exclusive reference.

Rules of thumb
  • Use &x to lend, &mut x to lend for writing. The callee's signature tells you which it needs.
  • *r is a place, so *r = v, &*r, and (*r).f all work; for fields, r.f is the same as (*r).f.
  • Bind a call result before keeping a borrow of it; borrowing one just for a call, f(&make()), is fine.
  • == on references asks whether they point at the same thing, not whether the values are equal; compare *a == *b for values.
← §08 Aliasing: shared and exclusive accessTop§10 Lifetimes and temporal validity →

§10Lifetimes and temporal validity

Governing specification file: spec/10-temporal-validity.md

A reference is checked statically where the escape is visible and dynamically everywhere else; either way it never outlives its target.

A reference must never outlive the object it refers to. CobaltC enforces this with two layers: a lexical check that rejects the obvious escapes before the program runs, and a use-time check that catches everything else as diag.stale-binding at the first use of a dead reference. No lifetime annotations exist; the language decides validity from where things are declared.

A reference cannot leave its referent's scope

If a reference to a local is returned from the function, or stored into a variable declared in an enclosing block, it is rejected statically as diag.reference-escapes-scope.

The corrected form returns the value itself: fn ok() : i32 { i32 x = 1; x }.

When the escape is not lexically visible (the reference is stored through another reference, into an aggregate the checker cannot see the owner of, or through a call), the static rule does not fire and the run-time check takes over. The program is still rejected, just later.

Returning references from functions

A function may return a reference when it has exactly one reference-typed parameter: the result is understood to point into whatever that argument pointed at, and callers are checked accordingly. This is the shape of every library accessor (Vec::index_shared, Rc::get). A function with zero or several reference parameters may not return a reference (diag.lifetime-elision-ambiguous); compose single-reference helpers instead, or return an owned value.

Because y above is known to borrow from pr, a later pr.a = 3; while y is still in use is an aliasing conflict (§08), exactly as if you had written auto y = &pr.a;.

Growth invalidates element references

A Vec may move its elements to a new buffer when it grows. A reference to an element obtained before a push that reallocates is stale afterwards. Where the checker can see both the borrow and the push in one function, it rejects the program; where it cannot (the push happens through a reference parameter, say), the stale reference faults at its next use. Either way it does not read freed memory.

Rules of thumb
  • Return values, not references, unless the function has exactly one reference parameter and the result points into it.
  • Do not store a reference in a variable that outlives the block where the referent was declared.
  • Re-fetch element references after any call that may grow or shrink a Vec.
  • If you see diag.stale-binding, ask what ended the referent: a scope exit, a move, a drop, or a reallocation.
← §09 ReferencesTop§11 Initialisation →

§11Initialisation

Governing specification file: spec/11-initialization.md

Every variable is written before it is read, on every path, and every aggregate is built whole; constants name values known before the program runs.

Reading storage that has never been written is undefined behaviour in C. In CobaltC it is impossible in a well-formed program: a variable declared without an initialiser must be assigned on every path before it is read, and the check is static. Aggregates are always initialised whole.

Declarations

FormMeaning
T x = e;declare x of type T, initialised from e (which is checked against T)
auto x = e;declare x with the type of e
T x;declare x uninitialised; the type is required because there is nothing to infer from
Name { f1, f2 } = e;destructure a struct: bind each field to its name and consume the struct

Initialising from a plain value copies it; from a resource, moves it; from a temporary such as a struct literal or a call result, adopts it.

One name, one declaration per block

A block declares a name once. A second i32 total further down the same block is diag.duplicate-local, which says where the first one is: to change the variable, assign to it (total = 10;); for a value of another type, give it another name. A function's parameters count as declared in its body, and so do the names a foreach, a for header, a match arm or an if-pattern binds for the block they govern, so fn f(i32 n) { i32 n = n * 2; } is rejected too: write n = n * 2;.

A block inside it may reuse the name: the inner variable shadows the outer one until the inner block ends, and the outer one is untouched. Separate blocks, successive loops and separate match arms each have their own names, and a local may take the name of a function or a constant (a program's own names never clash with names added to std later). Languages differ here: Rust lets any declaration shadow, Java and C# forbid shadowing a local even from an inner block; CobaltC follows C and C++. Every local can already be assigned, so a second declaration in the same block would only hide a mistake.

Constants

const τ NAME = e; names a value, at the top level of any module or inside a function (below). NAME can be used wherever its value could, with the visibility, export, import and qualified paths of any item. e must be a constant expression: literals, other constants, operators, struct, array and variant literals of constant expressions and their fields and elements (SCREEN.w, PRIMES[2]), a function's name, and the pure intrinsics (min_value, sizeof, widen, …). A constant cannot be a resource, cannot depend on itself, and cannot be assigned to or borrowed; an overflow in computing one is reported at the constant, before the program runs. Integer, float, bool and str constants cost nothing at run time: each use becomes the literal.

A constant is typed exactly as a declaration τ x = e; would be: in const u64 MIB = 1024 * 1024; the literals are u64s, and an initializer that overflows its type, such as const i32 BIG = 65536 * 65536;, is rejected at the constant. const auto NAME = e; takes its type from e, as auto x = e; does: const auto MIB = KIB * KIB; is a u64 when KIB is, and a bare literal is an i32 (or an f64). When e alone does not settle a type — None, say — write the type.

A constant can also be declared inside a function, as a statement: const u8 LIMIT = 200;. It is the same kind of constant, but its name is scoped like a local: it can be used from its declaration to the end of its block, and an inner block can declare another constant or a variable of the same name, which hides it there (in its own block, a second declaration of the name is diag.duplicate-local, above). A local variable, even one set from a literal, is not a constant — any later statement could change it — so static_assert cannot use it; name the value with const when you want the check made before the program runs. A local constant's initializer can use other constants, but not a local variable or the function's type parameters.

const means known when the program is compiled

A const can never change: assigning to it, or borrowing it with &mut, is rejected when the program is compiled. A constant is not a variable at all, but stands for its value, so assigning to it is like assigning to a literal. Copying its value out is fine: i32 y = LIMIT; gives a variable y, which can change, while LIMIT stays as it is.

What makes it a constant is when its value is known: before the program runs, like const in Rust, Go and C# or constexpr in C++. That differs from C, C++, Java or JavaScript, where const (or final) often marks a variable that is set once, at run time, and never reassigned. const usize N = arg_count(); is diag.const-not-constant, because the value is only known once the program runs.

CobaltC has no read-only local variables either: every local can be assigned. It does not need them for safety, because every change to a variable shows where it happens. Only two things can change a local: an assignment to its name in its own function, or an exclusive reference to it, &mut x, which must be written out where it is made. A function given &x or a copy of x cannot change it; while a shared reference to it is in use, nothing can (diag.aliasing-conflict, §8); and threads share changing state only through a mutex. So to see whether x can change, look in its function for x = and &mut x. To lend a value without letting it change, lend it with &.

Definite assignment

The analysis is purely about the function's own control flow: it does not know that c happens to be true. If it cannot prove a write on some path, the program is rejected (this is one of the few checks where "unknown" means rejected rather than "check at run time").

Aggregates are initialised whole

You cannot declare a struct uninitialised and then fill its fields one by one. A struct literal supplies every field at once; after that, individual fields can be assigned freely.

Destructuring a struct

This is the only pattern form outside match and the pattern conditions of if and while (§14). It names fields of the struct, each once, in any order, and consumes the struct: a resource field moves out to its new binding, a plain one is copied. It is how a struct gives up a resource it holds (the library's String::into_bytes uses it to hand back the Vec<u8>), since a resource field cannot otherwise be moved out of a struct that lives on. field : name binds a field to another name, so two values of one type can be taken apart side by side, and a final .. stands for the fields not named: they are not bound, and those holding resources are destroyed when the block ends. Naming a field twice, or leaving one out without .., is a type error, and a struct with its own destructor cannot be destructured, since the destructor would then run on a struct whose fields had left it (diag.move-out-of-field).

Rules of thumb
  • Prefer T x = e; or auto x = e;. Declare uninitialised only when the value genuinely comes from a branch, and then assign in every branch.
  • Build structs with a literal that names every field. Assign fields afterwards if needed.
  • auto needs an initialiser it can learn a type from; auto v = Vec::new(); is rejected because T is unknown (§12).
← §10 Lifetimes and temporal validityTop§12 The type system →

§12The type system

Governing specification file: spec/12-type-system.md

Nominal types, no coercions, monomorphic generics (one copy per use with concrete types) with five built-in bounds, and local inference that only flows downward.

CobaltC's type system is deliberately plain: every type is exactly what it is declared to be, nothing converts to anything else, and generics are templates instantiated with concrete types. What it gives you in return is that the type of every expression is decidable from the text, and that a function signature is a complete statement of what the function may do with its arguments.

The built-in types

TypeValuesResource?
integers, f32, f64, boolnumbers and truth values (§06)no
strtext: a valid UTF-8 byte sequence, written "…"; a whole value like an integer, not a reference and not owned (§21)no
void (type) / () (value)the unit type; the type of assignments, of if without else, of loops and of functions with no return type. Written void in type position and () as a value.no
ref<T, shared>, ref<T, exclusive>references (§09)no
rawptr<T>raw addresses (§20)no
array<T, N>N values of T in a row, N a constant expression (§16)if T is
slice<T, shared>, slice<T, exclusive>a borrowed run of elements of an array or Vec (§16)no
fn(T1, T2) : Rfunction valuesno
handle<T>, mutex<T>, guard<T>threads and locks (§19)yes
struct, enumuser-declared aggregates (§16)if marked resource or any part is
bitstructnamed runs of bits packed into one unsigned integer, u8 to u128 (§16)no
neverthe type of return, break and continue: an expression that never yields a value, accepted wherever any type is expectedn/a

Nominal, exact, no coercions

Two types are the same only if they have the same name and the same type arguments. ref<i32, shared> and ref<i32, exclusive> are different types. There is no subtyping and no implicit conversion anywhere: not between integer widths, not from T to ref<T, m>, not from Option<T> to T. This applies to arguments too. A literal is not an exception but a different thing: it has no type of its own until its position gives it one, so u64 x = 5;, StringView v = "x"; and String s = "x"; type the literal (§21) rather than convert a value, and the same positions still reject an i32, a str or any other typed value.

A bare integer literal is the one flexible thing: takes_i64(5) is fine, because the literal takes its type from the parameter (§06).

Equality

== and != are defined for numbers, bool, (), str (bytewise), references (identity), raw pointers (address), and for structs, arrays and enums whose parts are all comparable (element by element; enums must have the same variant and equal payloads). They are not defined for function values or for anything that is a resource, with one exception: two Strings compare by their text.

< <= > >= order numbers, bool (false before true), and text: two strs, two Strings or two StringViews, by their bytes, a prefix first (for UTF-8 that is code point order). A String operand is not copied or moved: it is borrowed for the comparison, as &s would be, so it stays usable afterwards.

Generics

Functions, structs and enums can take type parameters. Generics are monomorphic: each use with a different set of concrete types is a separate copy of the declaration, compiled (or, in the interpreter, run) as if you had written it out with those types: identity(5) and identity(2.5) below call two functions, one for i32 and one for f64. So there is no run-time type information, no boxing and no indirect call at call sites; the cost is one copy per combination of types used. Inside a generic body a value of a type parameter T can be stored, passed, returned, referenced and moved. To do more with it — compare it, add it — give T a bound (below).

Bounds

A function's type parameter may carry one of six bounds, written after a colon: fn max<T: ordered>(T a, T b) : T. Each of the first four names a fixed set of types and the operators every one of them has, and each includes the ones before it; clone says a value of T can be copied (below); plain that its bytes mean the same anywhere (§20):

BoundSatisfied byAllows on a T
eqintegers, floats, bool, str, String; and every key type: a struct or enum whose fields (payloads) are all integers, bool, str, String or such types (D-0110, D-0271)== !=
orderedthe samealso < <= > >=
numberintegers, floatsalso + - * / %, unary -, += and the like; integer literals
integerintegersalso & | ^ ~, << >>
cloneeverything above; String, Rc<T>, Box<T: clone>, Vec<T: clone>, the hash tables; a type with its own T::clone; a struct or enum whose fields are all clone (D-0116)clone(&x): an independent copy
plainnumbers, bool, raw pointers, simd, and arrays, structs or enums of those: bytes that mean the same anywhere (no resource, reference, handle, mutex, guard, function value or str)none of its own; what Vec::from_raw and copy_to_raw move across raw memory (§20)
Note
Built-in bounds describe compiler-defined capabilities. They are not user-extensible traits: there is no way to declare a new bound. Your own struct or enum satisfies clone — by its fields, or by a fn T::clone(ref<T, shared> self) : T you declare, recognised by its name as T::drop is — and eq and ordered when it is a key type (D-0271): its == is field-by-field equality and its < the order Vec::sort gives it, field by field in declaration order, an enum by variant order and then payload. So a < b holds exactly when Vec::sort puts a before b, and a == b exactly when a hash table treats them as one key. It never satisfies number or integer, and a type with a float field satisfies nothing but clone and plain: to combine values of your own types in generic code, or order a struct otherwise than by its fields, pass the operation in as a function value, as Vec::sort_by takes less.

The body is checked once against the bound: a + b in a function whose T is only ordered is diag.unbounded-type-parameter. Each call is checked for a type that satisfies it: largest of a struct with a float field is diag.type-mismatch, and the message names the field. Each use is also checked at its concrete type, so -x at T = u32 is still rejected there. Structs and enums take no bounds; put them on the functions that use the operations.

clone(&x) copies a value of any clone type: a plain one by reading it, String and the containers by their own clone, and a struct or enum of clone fields by a copy the compiler derives, field by field. A resource type — one with a destructor — declares its own T::clone or has none, because only it knows how to copy what it manages. Generic code says what it needs with the bound:

Inference is local and downward. A type parameter is found from, in order: an explicit type argument (identity<i64>(5)), the type of an argument in the same call, or the expected type where the call appears (a declared variable type, a parameter type, a field type). An unsuffixed literal argument comes last: it takes the type the other arguments or the expected type give its parameter, so with i64 x, pick(true, 0, x) makes T an i64 and the 0 with it; only when nothing else fixes T does a literal's own default (i32, f64) decide. Nothing is ever inferred from how a value is used later, so a call that fixes nothing is rejected:

The same holds when the call is an argument to another generic call. Mutex::new<T> is one: with auto nothing reaches it, so nothing reaches the Vec::new() inside it either. Give the outer binding its type and both are fixed.

auto and the expected type

auto x = e; gives x the type of e. Since inference is downward only, auto works whenever e has a type of its own: a literal (i32/f64 by default), an arithmetic expression, a call whose type parameters are already fixed, a struct literal with a concrete type. Where e needs help (Vec::new()), write the type on the left instead: auto m = Mutex::new(HashMap::new()); cannot know the map's types, but mutex<HashMap<String, i64>> m = Mutex::new(HashMap::new()); can. The branches of an if or match share one type, and a branch that is only a literal takes it from the others: in auto n = if (big) { count } else { 0 }; with count : i64, the 0 is an i64.

Rules of thumb
  • Write the type you mean; the language will not adjust it for you. Convert integers with widen/narrow, and take references explicitly.
  • Use auto freely for values whose type is obvious from the right-hand side, and a written type for empty containers and generic constructors.
  • Keep generic code to plumbing (containers, wrappers, moving values around). Anything that computes on T needs a concrete type.
  • A void function returns (); you may write : void explicitly or leave the return type off.
← §11 InitialisationTop§13 Expressions →

§13Expressions

Governing specification file: spec/13-expression-semantics.md

Places versus values, strict left-to-right evaluation, and the operators.

CobaltC has a small expression language with a fixed evaluation order and a clear line between places (things you can assign to or borrow) and values. Almost everything is an expression, including blocks, if and match, which is what lets you write i32 x = if (c) { 1 } else { 2 };.

Places and values

A place is a variable name, a field access e.f, an index e[i], or a dereference *r. A place can be read (yielding its value), written (place = e), borrowed (&place, &mut place), or projected further. Everything else, such as a literal, an arithmetic result, a call result or a struct literal, is a value or a temporary. Reading a place that holds a resource is not allowed (that would copy the resource, §07); such a place may only be moved, borrowed, or destructured.

Evaluation order

Every expression is evaluated strictly left to right: the left operand before the right, the callee before its arguments, arguments in written order, struct-literal fields in written order. Assignment evaluates the target place first, then the value. && and || short-circuit: the right operand runs only when needed.

Expressions that produce values

Tip
A block, if, while or match used as a statement needs no semicolon after its closing brace. When one of them is the right-hand side of a declaration or assignment, the statement as a whole still ends with ;, as in i32 x = if (c) { 1 } else { 2 };.

Operator precedence

From tightest to loosest binding. Comparison is non-associative: a < b < c is a syntax error, and a < b == c needs parentheses.

LevelOperatorsNotes
postfixe.f e[i] e(args) e?field, index, call, propagate
unary-e !e ~e &e &mut e *enegate, boolean not, bitwise not, borrow, dereference
multiplicative* / %left-associative
additive+ -left-associative; p + n on a rawptr is pointer offset (§20)
shift<< >>the right operand is a u32
bitwise and&
bitwise xor^
bitwise or|
comparison== != < <= > >=non-associative
logical and&&short-circuit
logical or||short-circuit
assignment= += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>=right-associative; the left side must be a place

x op= e is x = x op e with x evaluated once: the same types, the same overflow check (x += 1 can overflow), the same write rules. Evaluating the place once matters only when it contains a call, as in *Vec::index_exclusive(&mut v, i) += 1, which calls index_exclusive once. There is no ++ or --; write += 1.

Watch out
Shifts bind tighter than the bitwise operators, as in C and Rust: hi << 8 | lo is (hi << 8) | lo. Unlike C, the bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons, so x & 1 == 0 parses as (x & 1) == 0. When in doubt, add parentheses.
Rules of thumb
  • Use if, match and blocks as values instead of declaring a variable and assigning in each branch.
  • Side effects in one operand are visible to the next: order is defined, so you may rely on it, but readers will thank you for not making them.
  • Parenthesise mixed comparisons and bitwise expressions.
← §12 The type systemTop§14 Control flow and scopes →

§14Control flow and scopes

Governing specification file: spec/14-control-flow.md

Blocks, if, while, for, foreach, break and continue; scope exit as the moment of destruction; and the fixed line between compile-time and run-time checks.

Control flow is C's if, while and for, without switch and goto, plus expression-valued if and match and a foreach over collections. What is new is how carefully the language ties scope to destruction, and the precise line between what the compiler proves and what the run time checks.

Blocks and scopes

A block { … } opens a scope. Variables declared in it die when it ends, in reverse order; resources are destroyed at that point (§07); references held by those variables end too. A block is an expression: its value is its trailing expression, or () if there is none. Every statement is a scope of its own for temporaries: a value created during a statement and not stored anywhere is destroyed at the semicolon.

if and else

if (cond) { … } else { … } with mandatory parentheses and mandatory braces. else if chains as expected. An if without else has type void; an if used as a value needs both arms, of the same type.

The condition may also be a pattern test, if (Some(x) = e) { … } else { … }: it means match (e) { Some(x) : { … }, _ : { … } }, so x exists in the first block only, e is consumed exactly as that match would consume it, and the whole if can be a value. Any match pattern works — nested (Ok(Some(l))), a literal (if (0 = n)), a qualified variant — as long as it can fail: a bare name on the left of = is the assignment it always is, which is not a bool and is rejected, so if (x = e) never silently tests anything. A match stays the form when both cases do work, and the only form that checks every case is handled.

while, for, break, continue

while (cond) { … } loops while cond holds; for (init; cond; step) { … } is C's counted loop: init runs once (a declaration there belongs to the loop), cond is tested before each iteration, and step runs after each one. Any of the three may be left out; a missing cond is true, so for (;;) loops until a break. The body is a fresh scope each iteration, so anything declared inside it is destroyed before the next test. break exits the innermost loop; continue goes to its next iteration, running a for's step first. Both are typed never and must appear inside a loop. A body is always a block, so C's trap for (…); (an empty loop, then a block that runs once) is a syntax error here, and the message says to remove the ;.

A while condition may be a pattern test too: while (Some(x) = e) { … } is while (true) { match (e) { Some(x) : { … }, _ : break } } — e is evaluated again each time round, the body runs with x bound while the pattern matches, and the first value that does not match ends the loop. That last point matters for a Result: while (Ok(Some(line)) = read_line()) stops at the end of input and on a read error alike, which is the loop's written decision; a loop that must tell them apart keeps the match.

Loops that only end by returning. A while (true) that no break leaves can end only by return, a fault or exit, so nothing after it ever runs: its type is never, like return's (D-0175). A function may therefore end with such a loop and needs no value after it. A break inside a nested loop leaves only that loop and does not count; a break that leaves the while (true) itself makes it an ordinary loop again, after which the function must still give its value. Only the literal true has this meaning: the compiler does not look into a condition that merely happens to stay true. There is no separate loop keyword; while (true) is the way to say "forever".

foreach

foreach (x in c) { … } visits every element of a Vec, an array, a slice, a HashSet or a HashMap, in order: by index for a Vec or an array, in insertion order for a set or a map. How the loop holds the collection is written at the loop, the same three ways a function takes a value:

WrittenEach element isAfterwards
foreach (x in c)the element itself, moved out of cc is gone: the loop consumed it
foreach (x in &c)a shared reference, ref<T, shared>: read itc is unchanged and usable
foreach (x in &mut c)an exclusive reference: *x = … changes the elementc is usable, with its changes

Use &c most of the time. A second name gives the position: foreach (i, x in &v) has i : usize. A HashMap is always looped over with two names, the key and the value: foreach (k, v in &m), or three to have the position too, foreach (i, k, v in &m). printf prints what a reference refers to, so printf("%d", x) works with x a ref<i32, shared>; elsewhere write *x for the number.

The loop's borrow of the collection lasts the whole loop, so a body that tries to change the collection itself (push to it, clear it) is rejected before the program runs, the same aliasing rule as anywhere else. There is no iterator invalidation to debug. A consuming loop left early, by break, return or a fault, destroys the elements it had not reached, exactly once.

An array of plain values, such as array<i32, 5>, is copied by the by-value form: foreach (i, e in arr) walks a copy, so arr is neither borrowed nor used up, a write to arr[j] in the body is allowed (and not seen by e), and arr is still there afterwards. To change the elements themselves, loop over &mut arr and write through the reference: *e = …. While that loop runs, arr is borrowed by it, so reach the elements through e, not through arr[j].

Counting with a range

foreach (x in lo..hi) counts from lo up to, not including, hi, the same way &a[lo..hi] takes elements lo up to hi. So 0..n runs exactly n times, and 1..10 stops at 9. A second name gives the position, counted from 0: foreach (i, x in lo..hi). Both bounds are evaluated once, lo first. If hi is not above lo, the body never runs.

x has the bounds' integer type. A plain number takes the other bound's type, so with u8 top, 0..top counts in u8. Two plain numbers are usize, so the counter can index an array or a Vec directly; for a negative range, give one bound a type: -3..0: i32. Bounds of two different types are rejected rather than converted. A range can end at its type's largest value without overflowing, because the counter never passes hi.

A range to count over is written only in a foreach (a slice's lo..hi, §16, is the same notation for elements). It is not a value you can store, and it has no inclusive form or step. To count down or in steps, use a for loop.

Early exit and unwinding

return, break, continue, and a run-time fault all leave scopes the same way: every statement scope and block between here and the target is exited in order, destroying what each one owns. A return e first moves e out so it survives the unwinding. You never have to write cleanup code on an early exit.

What is checked when

Many rules in this guide say a program is "rejected" in one example and "faults at run time" in another. The boundary is fixed by the language, not left to the compiler's cleverness, so that every implementation accepts and rejects the same programs. A compiler may prove more than this checker does and leave out the run-time checks it has proved unnecessary (that is what cobc does; see the performance chapter), but it may not accept a program the language rejects or reject one it accepts: coby --check is the reference, and what it accepts is the language. Within one function body, the checker tracks a few facts about each variable: whether it has been moved from, whether it has been initialised, which references were visibly borrowed from it, and whether a reference to it has been handed somewhere the checker cannot follow (a call, a field, a thread). At each checked operation the outcome is one of three:

OutcomeWhenEffect
proventhe tracked facts guarantee the conditionno run-time check
refutedthe tracked facts guarantee it failsthe program is rejected (a static diagnostic)
unknownthe facts do not decide (the value came from a call, a loop merged two states, a reference passed through a parameter)the run-time check runs, and faults if it fails (a dynamic diagnostic)

The analysis looks only at the current function and only at literals for value ranges. So 2147483647 + 1 is refuted statically, add(2147483647, 1) is checked when add runs, and borrowing x twice exclusively in one function is refuted while doing so through two reference parameters is checked at the use. Three exceptions are stricter: definite assignment (§11), a use of a variable that may have been moved (§7), and reference escape (§10) reject on "unknown" rather than deferring.

Rules of thumb
  • Let scopes do your cleanup. Open a block to bound a borrow or a lock; close it to release.
  • A while body is re-entered fresh each iteration; declare per-iteration variables inside it.
  • Prefer trailing expressions to return at the end of a function; use return for early exits.
  • If a diagnostic says static, the checker saw the problem in the text; if dynamic, it saw it when the values arrived. Both are the same rule.

§15Functions and closures

Governing specification file: spec/15-function-semantics.md

Signatures that state the whole contract, associated functions, function values, and closures with checked capture lists.

Functions in CobaltC carry their whole contract in the signature. A parameter's type says whether the function takes ownership, may only look, or may modify. Closures are ordinary structs that capture what they use, and the capture list is checked, not trusted.

Declaring and calling

Recursion needs nothing special, and its depth is limited only by the stack. Every implementation allows at least 10 000 nested calls, and both tools allow far more: they run a program and each of its threads on a large stack. A call beyond the limit is not a crash but a fault at the call, diag.stack-exhausted, so a recursion that runs away ends with a diagnostic like any other failure.

A parameter list and an argument list may end with a comma, as array and struct literals may: handy when a long call is split one argument per line. A comma is never the whole list: f(,) is a syntax error.

What a parameter type promises

Parameter typeThe caller writesThe callee mayAfter the call
plain T (numbers, plain structs)f(x)use its own copythe caller's x is unchanged
resource T (Vec<i32>, handle<T>, …)f(v)own it: mutate, move on, or let it be destroyed at its scope endthe caller's v is stale
ref<T, shared>f(&x)read through itthe borrow is released; x is unchanged
ref<T, exclusive>f(&mut x)read and write through it, but not destroy or move xthe borrow is released; x may have changed

Function values

A function type is written fn(T1, T2) : R (or fn(T1) for a void result). A parameter of that type accepts a function with that signature, or a closure with the same parameters and result. Function values cannot be compared.

A closure's type is fn(parameters) : result, the result being what its body gives. Where a fn type is expected, as when a closure is declared fn(u32) : u32 f = … or passed to such a parameter, the body is checked against that result, and its literals take that type. A closure declared with auto takes its body's own type: [](u32 x) { 1 } gives an i32, as auto y = 1 does. A closure can be stored like any value: in a variable, a field, a Vec<fn(…) : …> or a Box, and called from there.

A function value owns the closure it holds and destroys it when it ends. Copying the value (g = f, passing it by value) copies the closure with its captures, so each copy keeps its own state. The one exception is a closure that owns a resource, such as a move closure that captured a String: copying it would duplicate the resource, so it moves instead, and the value it came from is left empty. Calling an empty function value is diag.stale-binding; the function type does not say what its closure owns, so this is found when the program runs. Calling through a reference, a field or an element ((*f)(x), (t.run)(), (fs[i])()) calls the value where it is and moves nothing.

Closures

Functions do not nest: a fn declared inside another function is a syntax error, unless it is a function of a type declared in the same block (fn T::name, §16). A function needed only inside another is written there as a closure, which can also use the variables around it.

A closure is written [captures](params) { body }, in the style of a C++ lambda. The bracket must list exactly the outer variables the body uses, no more and no fewer; it is documentation that the compiler checks (diag.capture-list-mismatch). How each variable is captured is decided by the body, not the list: a variable the body only reads is captured by shared reference; one the body writes, borrows exclusively, or moves is captured by exclusive reference. Prefix move to capture by value instead, moving resources into the closure. The result type is taken from the body, or from the fn(…) : R the closure is passed as; write it after the parameters, as for a function, when neither says enough: [](i64 a) : i64 { 0 }.

A closure that captures by reference holds those borrows for as long as the closure object lives, so the captured variables are subject to the usual aliasing rules until it goes out of scope: a closure that writes total blocks every other use of total while it exists. Put such closures in a block, or use move. Calling a closure borrows it shared for the call: its writes go through the captures, which are checked as any reference is, so a closure that writes a capture cannot be called through a shared reference to it.

A move closure that changes a value it captured changes the closure itself, so a call borrows it exclusively. Such a counter is called from its own binding; called while a shared reference to it lives, the call is diag.aliasing-conflict (reported before the program runs when that reference is certainly still in use), and called through a shared reference it is diag.borrow-exceeds-source.

Generic functions

fn name<T>(...) declares type parameters; see §12 for what a body may do with T and how T is inferred at each call.

main

A program is a set of declarations with exactly one main at the top level, taking no parameters: fn main(), or fn main() : u8. Execution is the evaluation of main(); the program's observable behaviour is its termination outcome (success or a named fault) plus the sequence of extern calls it makes.

A main that returns a u8 sets the program's exit status; fn main() exits with 0. Returning from main runs every destructor still pending and waits for every thread, as leaving any block does, so the status is reported only after all of that. A fault still ends the program with its diagnostic instead. The arguments the program was started with come from arg_count() and arg(i) (§21); argument 0 is the first one after the program, not the program's name.

Run with no argument, the same program prints its usage line and exits with status 2. A main with parameters, or returning anything other than u8, is rejected with diag.no-main.

Rules of thumb
  • Choose the parameter kind that says the least: a shared reference if the function only reads, an exclusive reference if it modifies, by value only if it needs to keep the thing.
  • Return values rather than out-parameters; a struct or an enum is cheap to return.
  • List every captured variable in the closure brackets and let the compiler tell you if you got it wrong.
  • Use move closures for anything that outlives the current block or runs on another thread.

§16Structs, arrays, enums and match

Governing specification file: spec/16-aggregates.md

The four aggregate kinds, how they nest, and exhaustive matching over enums with payloads.

CobaltC has four aggregate kinds: structs (named fields), bitstructs (named runs of bits packed into one unsigned integer), arrays (a fixed number of elements) and enums (one of several variants, each with an optional payload). They compose freely, and all but bitstructs generically. match is how you take an enum apart, and it must handle every variant.

Structs

Field initialisers use C99's designated form .name = value. Fields are private to the module that declares the struct unless marked export (§17). A struct with no fields is allowed. Mark a struct resource if it manages something beyond its fields (§07).

bitstruct: named bits of one integer

A bitstruct is a struct whose fields are runs of bits of one unsigned integer, its backing type: bitstruct Instr : u32 { op : 6; rd : 5; rs : 5; imm : 16; }. The fields are laid out from the low bit up in declaration order and must fill the backing type exactly (name the unused bits, pad : 3;). Each field has the smallest unsigned type that holds its width — u8 up to 8 bits, u16 up to 16, and so on — and is read and written like any field, i.op, i.imm = 500. A write that does not fit its field faults with diag.narrowing-overflow, or is rejected outright when the value is a literal; nothing is ever truncated. Instr::bits(i) is the whole integer and Instr::from_bits(w) the fields of one, both total. A bitstruct is a plain value: copied by a read, clone, equal by its bits, a HashMap key, and its bytes in raw memory are the integer's. A field has no address of its own, so it cannot be borrowed — borrow the whole value — and a bitstruct is not taken apart by destructuring. Byte order is not its concern: Vec::push_le and push_be write it out (D-0119), and an unsafe extern fn takes Instr::bits(i).

Arrays

array<T, N> holds exactly N elements; N is a constant expression — a literal, a const name (m::N too), or + - * / % & | ^ << >> ~ ( ) over them, folded before the program runs (D-0126); outside parentheses > ends it, so Vec<array<u8, N * 2>> reads as expected. The literal form is [a, b, c]. Indexing takes a usize and is bounds-checked: a literal index out of range is rejected statically, a computed one faults at run time with diag.index-out-of-bounds. Arrays of plain elements are plain (copied on assignment); an array of resources is a resource.

[v; N] makes an array of N copies of v, which is evaluated once. N is written as in the type array<T, N>, a constant expression: a number, a constant (const usize W = 24; then array<u8, W> and [0; W], in this module or, qualified, a visible one of another, array<u8, screen::W>), or arithmetic on them ([0; W * 2]). Because the value is copied, its type must be plain: a String or other resource, a reference, or a function value cannot be repeated (diag.read-of-resource or diag.type-mismatch); build such arrays element by element, or use a Vec.

Arrays of arrays

CobaltC has no separate multidimensional array type. An array's element can itself be an array, so a grid, a cube, or anything with more dimensions is the one constructor used again: array<array<i64, 3>, 2> is an array of 2 elements, each an array<i64, 3>. The same holds for the literal forms, [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] and [[0; 3]; 2], and for auto, which infers the nesting from the literal.

Two directions are worth keeping straight:

  • The type reads from the inside out. In array<array<array<i64, 3>, 2>, 4> the innermost array<i64, 3> is a row of 3 numbers, the next array<…, 2> holds 2 such rows (a block), and the outermost array<…, 4> holds 4 blocks. The length written last is the outermost one.
  • Indexing and loops go from the outside in. cube[i][j][k] picks block i (below 4), then row j of it (below 2), then element k of that row (below 3). Nested loops follow the same order: the outer loop walks the blocks, the innermost the elements of one row, so the elements are visited in the order they lie in memory.

Each index is checked against its own length. Because every level is an ordinary array, cube[1] is a whole block and cube[1][0] a whole row, values you can copy, pass and loop over. Writing those inner types out gets long; where the type is clear from the right-hand side, auto reads better. To print every value, nest one foreach per level: foreach (i, block in &cube) borrows each block, and the loop inside it over block borrows each row of that block, so nothing is copied.

For a growable sequence use Vec<T> (§21). A Vec is indexed the same way, v[i]: it reads through Vec::index_shared, and writes (an assignment, &mut v[i]) through Vec::index_exclusive, so every rule about borrowing the Vec applies.

Slices

A slice is a borrowed run of consecutive elements of an array, a Vec, or another slice: &a[i..j] is elements i up to (not including) j, and &mut a[i..j] the same for writing. Inside the brackets, $ stands for the length of what is being indexed, so &a[0..$] is all of it and &a[$ - 3 .. $] the last three, and v[$ - 1] is a Vec's last element. $ is a usize like any index, so v[$ - 1] of an empty v is an overflow fault, never a wrapped-around index.

The type is slice<T, shared> or slice<T, exclusive>. One parameter of that type takes any array, any Vec, or part of either, so a function need not be written once per container or per array length. slice_len(s) is its length; s[i] is bounds-checked; foreach works over it. A slice is a borrow like a reference: while it lives, the elements it views cannot be changed except through it, its source cannot be pushed to or popped from, and a slice of a local cannot be returned.

A slice borrows only its own elements. Two slices of one array or Vec conflict only if their ranges share an element, so a buffer can be split into parts that are each written through their own exclusive slice, at the same time: the halves of a divide-and-conquer algorithm, or one part per thread. What reaches the whole source (&mut v, Vec::push) still conflicts with every live slice of it.

Vectors: simd<τ, N>

A simd<τ, N> is N numbers that one processor instruction works on together: four f32s in a 16-byte register, thirty-two u8s in a 32-byte one. Arithmetic on two vectors applies to every lane at once, so a loop that steps eight elements at a time does eight elements' work per step. The type is portable: cobc compiles it to the target's vector instructions (SSE, AVX or NEON, chosen by -march), or to pairs of narrower ones where the target has no register that wide, and coby runs it lane by lane with the same results.

Allowed
Lanesan integer type (not i128/u128), f32 or f64
ShapesN a power of two from 2, and N × size 8, 16, 32 or 64 bytes: simd<f32, 4>, simd<f32, 8>, simd<u8, 16>, simd<i64, 2>, simd<f64, 8> …
Making onean array literal or [x; N] where a simd is expected; simd_load<V>(s, i) from a slice
Lanesv[i] read and assigned (checked); never borrowed
Operators+ - * (and / for floats), & | ^ ~ and shifts for integers, == != on the whole; both operands one simd type
Lane-wisesimd_lt and kin give masks; simd_select, simd_any, simd_all; simd_min, simd_max
Reductionssimd_sum, simd_reduce_min, simd_reduce_max, from lane 0 to the last

Integer lanes are checked as integers are everywhere: if any lane of a + b overflows, the program faults. Where wrapping is the intent, as in hashing or a sum that cannot overflow, wrapping_add, wrapping_mul and saturating_add take vectors too, and they are the fast path. Float lanes follow IEEE 754 with no fused multiply-add, and simd_sum adds left to right, so a result is the same bit for bit under both tools; it can differ from a scalar loop's, which adds in another order.

A comparison of two vectors is a mask: lanes of the same width holding -1 where the comparison holds and 0 where it does not. simd_select(m, a, b) takes each lane from a or b by the mask, which replaces a branch inside the loop.

How much a vector gains depends on the machine and the C compiler. On a processor with only 128-bit SSE registers, an 8-lane f32 dot product ran about twice as fast as the scalar loop with GCC and over three times as fast with Clang; with AVX2 (cobc -march=native on such a machine) the 8 lanes fit one register. Data far larger than the cache is limited by memory bandwidth whichever form you write.

Types declared inside a function

A struct, enum or bitstruct used by one function can be declared inside it, as a statement, and so can its functions, fn T::name(…) (a destructor too). It is an ordinary type whose name is scoped like a local: usable from its declaration to the end of its block. Two functions can each have their own Entry. A local type and its functions see module items and the local types and constants around them, but not the function's variables or type parameters; a plain local function is written as a closure (§15).

A bitstruct declared in a function is the same as one at module level: it gets its Name::bits and Name::from_bits, and its fields read and write in the same way. A packed header that one decoder reads can live inside that decoder.

Enums and match

An enum lists its variants; each may carry one payload type. Variant names are used bare (Cold(3), Fine) or qualified (Verdict::Fine) when two visible enums share a name. A variant with no payload behaves as if it carried ().

match (e) { … } compares the discriminant and runs the arm for that variant. Each arm is Variant(binder) : expression, for a payload, Variant : expression, for none, or _ : expression, as a catch-all; every arm ends with a comma. The arms must cover every variant or include _. Arms are expressions, so a match produces a value; use a block as the arm body for statements. Arms are tried in order and the first that fits is taken.

Nested patterns

Inside the parentheses, a pattern can say what the payload itself must be, as deep as needed: Ok(Some(line)) matches an Ok whose payload is a Some, and binds the Some's payload. A name there is a binder, unless it is a variant's name (Some(None)), and _ ignores that level. Since a variant has one payload, an arm binds one name, the innermost payload it reaches, unless that payload is a struct taken apart by a struct pattern (below). Every value must reach some arm (the error names one that does not, such as Ok(None)), and every arm must be reachable: an arm whose values all go to earlier arms is rejected, since it could never run.

Struct patterns

Where a binder could stand, a struct pattern can take the payload apart at once: Some(Question { name, end }) binds name and end, as Question { name, end } = q; would after binding q. The rules are destructuring's (§11): every field is named once, or .. stands for the rest; end : e binds a field to another name; and the fields are taken by value, so a String field moved out consumes the value matched, as any binder of a resource payload does. A struct pattern always fits, so it counts as a binder for exhaustiveness. It works in match arms and in if and while patterns. Through a reference (match (&o)) it is rejected: bind the payload and read its fields through it.

Literal patterns

A pattern can also be a literal: an integer (3, -1, 0x10), a byte (b'x'), true or false. It can stand alone, when the value being matched is an integer or a bool, or at the end of a nested pattern: Ok(0), Some(b'\n'). This is CobaltC's multi-way branch in place of switch, and it is checked: a literal must be of the type it is compared with, a repeated case is an arm that can never run, and an integer match needs a _ arm, since literals never list every value (true and false do cover a bool). Text is matched the same way: a match on a str, a String or a StringView takes text literals ("get" : …), compared byte for byte where the text is, so a String you match on is still yours afterwards; Some("quit") works inside a payload too, and if ("quit" = cmd) as a condition. Floats are not patterns. With that, patterns are _, a literal, a variant, and a variant with a pattern for its payload; there is nothing else to learn.

Ranges and several values

An arm names one pattern: there are no range patterns (10..15 : …) and no lists of alternatives (1, 4, 6 : … or 1 | 4 | 6 : …); each is a syntax error. Two forms cover these cases. To test a range, match on the test itself: the condition is a bool, and true and false cover it, so no _ arm is needed. Write the bounds as a range would mean them, the upper one left out (v < 15 for 10..15).

For several values that share an action, give each value its own arm, and put an action longer than a line in a function the arms call: the match still checks every literal's type and reports a repeated one. When the values are the whole question, match on the test instead, as for a range. For a longer list, keep the values in an array and ask contains, or in a HashSet when the list is built at run time. Text works the same way: one arm per word.

Binders and named constants

A name on its own is a pattern too. If it names a constant of integer or bool type, it is that constant's value, a literal by name (PUSH : …); if it names a variant, it is that variant; otherwise it is a new binding for the whole value, which matches anything, like _, and is usually the last arm (other : …). A binding of a resource moves it, as a payload binding does. Mistaking a constant for a binding cannot go unnoticed: a match on an integer then lacks _.

Matching through a reference

match (e) binds each payload by value: a plain one is copied, and a resource one (a String, a Vec, a Box) is moved out, which consumes the enum. To look at an enum without taking it apart, match a reference to it: match (&e) binds each payload as a shared reference, match (&mut e) as an exclusive one, through which the payload can be changed. A scrutinee that already is a reference, such as a function's ref<Expr, shared> parameter, binds in its own mode. The enum is not consumed, and the usual borrow rules apply to what is bound: nothing can replace the enum while a payload reference is still in use. This is how a tree built from Boxes (§21) is walked.

A nested pattern looks through a reference payload in the same way. HashMap::get gives an Option<ref<V, shared>>; when V is an enum, Some(Num(v)) matches its variant through the reference and binds v as a reference of that mode, so a lookup is taken apart in one match. A literal compares through a reference too: Some(0) against an Option<ref<u32, shared>>. The binder borrows what the reference borrows, so the map cannot change while v is in use.

An arm that takes the payload consumes the enum

If the enum carries a resource payload, an arm that binds that payload by value moves it into the binder and consumes the enum: if that arm ran, the scrutinee is stale afterwards. This is what makes match (Vec::pop(&mut v)) { Some(x) : …, None : … } hand you the popped element. An arm that takes nothing out — _, a payload-less variant, or Some(_) — leaves the scrutinee alone, so match (o) { None : …, _ : use(o) } is fine. To look inside and keep the enum whatever the arm, match on a reference to it (above).

Numeric codes

An enum without payloads can carry a number per variant, for a file format, a protocol or a C interface: enum Op : u8 { Add = 1, Sub, Mul = 10 }. The type after the colon is the code type, any integer type. A variant without = n takes the previous code plus one (the first, 0). Two variants may not share a code. The enum then has two associated functions: Op::code(e) gives a variant's code, and Op::from_code(n) gives Some(variant) for a code in use and None for any other.

Generic aggregates

struct Box<T> { T value; } and enum Maybe<T> { Just(T), Nothing } declare families of types. std's Option<T> and Result<T, E> are ordinary enums of exactly this kind (§21). Type arguments may be left off a literal when the declared type of the variable, parameter or field fixes them (§12).

Layout

A struct is laid out as C lays out the same members in the same order (D-0250): each field at the first offset its alignment allows after the previous one, and the end padded to the largest alignment. So C code given a rawptr<S> finds every field where its own offsetof says (§20). Arrays are contiguous with no padding; an enum is a discriminant of documented width followed by the largest payload, aligned. sizeof<T>() and alignof<T>() report the result (examples in §06, "Sizes and limits of types").

align(N) after a struct's name raises its alignment to N, a power of two up to 4096 (D-0251), and pads its size to a multiple of it, so every element of an array or Vec of it starts on an N boundary. It is C's alignas on a type. The usual reason is to give data that threads change a cache line of its own: two counters on one 64-byte line make the cores take the line from each other on every write, though they never touch the same counter. align raises and never lowers; a field gets an alignment by being of an aligned struct type.

Rules of thumb
  • Reach for an enum whenever a value is one of several cases; match forces you to handle each one.
  • Use _ sparingly: a wildcard arm silently absorbs variants you add later.
  • Give match arms a block body when they need statements, and remember the comma after each arm.
  • Build aggregates whole with a literal, then mutate fields as places.

§17Modules and name resolution

Governing specification file: spec/17-modules.md

module, export and import; re-export; private by default; a module's body may be another file; a fixed lookup order for every name.

Modules group declarations and control which names are visible where. They introduce no new semantics: ownership, borrowing and every other rule apply unchanged across module boundaries.

Declaring modules

module name { … } encloses any declarations, including nested modules. Everything is private by default: usable from its own module and the modules nested inside it. export on a declaration makes it usable from outside. An exported item inside a private module is only reachable where that module is.

Each declaration adds one qualified name (bank::fee, bank::Account::open, Shape::Circle), and a name may be added only once, so declaring fee twice in bank is diag.duplicate-item. The same simple name in two different modules is two different names. An associated function fn T::name belongs in the module that declares T; anywhere else it is diag.foreign-associated-fn, so no program can add to, or replace, the functions of std's Vec.

import

import a::b::name; lets name be used unqualified in the importing module. It creates no alias and no copy; it only extends name lookup. There is no import … as renaming: if two imports would give one name two meanings, qualify.

import m; naming a module does two things: m itself resolves, as with any import, and every item m exports, including the variants of its exported enums, can be used unqualified, except its submodules, which keep their paths (std::text) or are imported themselves. This is how programs use the standard library: import std;. A name is looked up in a fixed order: the module's own declarations first, then single-name imports, then module imports, then the enclosing modules. So a module's own printf wins over std::printf, which stays reachable by its full name. If two imported modules both export a name, using that name unqualified is diag.ambiguous-name; importing both is fine, so a module that gains an export never breaks a program that does not use it. An import acts only in the module that writes it: a nested module, or a module in a file of its own, writes its own import std;.

Re-export: export import

An import can be exported like any other declaration. export import p; in a module M does what import p; does, and also passes on what p brings in as M's own items: every item the module p exports, or the one item p names. A program that imports M then finds those names as if M had declared them, and M::name works too. They are the same items, not copies: a type passed on this way is one type under two paths. This is how a library divided into modules is still used with one import, and how std itself is built (§21): import std; brings in std::text, std::io and the rest because std re-exports each of them.

Only what is exported passes through: a private item never becomes reachable by being re-exported. A name the module already has for a different item is diag.duplicate-item; the same item arriving twice, or two modules re-exporting each other, is not an error.

Constants as items

A const declared at a module's top level is an item like a function: it is private unless marked export, it can be imported, and other modules name it by its path (config::LIMIT). Constants themselves, and the static_assert checks built on them, are described with declarations (§11) and with assertions (§18). The specification keeps their rules in its modules chapter (spec/17 §1a and §1b), because a constant is an item.

A module in another file

A module's body can be a separate file. module geo "./geometry.cb"; means exactly module geo { … } with the file's declarations as the body: the same visibility, the same import, the same lookup. The declaring file names the module; the other file's top level is anonymous, just as an inline body is. The path is relative to the directory of the file that writes it, so a file can itself declare file-backed modules with paths relative to its own location, and a library moves as a unit. Use forward slashes and stay inside the tree (no leading /, no ..); anything beyond that is up to the implementation.

Three things are rejected before anything runs: a path that names no file (diag.module-file-not-found), a file whose body would load itself again through some chain of declarations (diag.module-cycle), and one file named by two declarations (diag.module-file-duplicate — it would be two distinct modules and two distinct Rect types). A fn main in a loaded file is just the item geo::main; the program's entry is the root file's main, and a program with none is diag.no-main. Both implementations report a diagnostic inside a loaded file against that file and its own line.

A library in several files

Files and re-export (above) together give a library that is split across files but used with one import. Its root file declares the parts, keeps its helpers in a private module, and passes on what users should see: here every exported item of shapes, and cm alone from units. The helpers are usable everywhere inside the library and nowhere outside it, and the files can be reorganized later without changing any program that imports the root.

How a name is found

An unqualified name is first looked up as a local variable or parameter. Failing that, in this order: an item of the current module; an import in the current module whose last segment matches; an item of an enclosing module, outward to the root; finally a variant: first of the enums of this module, or else of the nearest enclosing module with one of that name, and only if there is none, of an imported enum. So your own enum Shape { …, Empty } keeps its bare Empty even though std's ParseError has an Empty too. And where a value is written, a type the earlier steps find is passed over, since a type is no value: your enum Report { File(u64), … } keeps its bare File(n) beside import std;, which exports the struct File, and File in a type position is still std's (D-0266). More than one candidate at a step is diag.ambiguous-name; none at all is diag.unbound-name. A qualified name a::b::c starts by resolving a the same way and then walks into it, checking visibility at the end.

Two special cases: an associated function declared as fn Type::name(…) is addressed as Type::name (or mod::Type::name from outside), and an enum's variants are addressable as Enum::Variant as well as bare.

Structs and fields across modules

A struct or enum declared in a module is an item like any other: export it to use it outside. Each field has its own visibility too; write export i32 x; for fields that callers may read and write directly, and leave the rest private to give the module full control over its invariants.

Naming a private field from outside its module — reading it, writing it, giving it in a struct literal, or destructuring it — is diag.name-not-visible, the same diagnostic as for a private function. Give the module a constructor function if callers need to build the struct.

There are no read-only (const) fields: in CobaltC const means a value known before the program runs (§11 constants), not "fixed once built". A field that other code may read but not change is a private field with an exported function that reads it. Only the module can then change it, which is also what keeps the module's invariant in one place.

Rules of thumb
  • Start every module with everything private; export only what callers need.
  • Prefer qualified calls (maths::square(x)) in code that reads like a library; import the handful of names you use constantly.
  • Module boundaries are not safety boundaries: unsafe is lexical (§20). To confine trusted code, keep the functions that wrap it un-exported.
  • Split a program across files with module m "./m.cb";, one file per module; keep paths relative and let the declaring file do the naming.
