RThe std reference

Every exported item of std: its declaration, its documentation and its examples, generated from the library's source.

Every item a program can use from std, module by module, with its declaration, what it does, and for some an example. The text is the /// documentation in impl/std itself (spec/22 §1), read by impl/tools/cobdoc.py when this page is built; each example is a unittest block of std (coby --unittest-std), run here as a program's main under both tools. The items both tools build in, which have no CobaltC body (printf, sqrt, exit, …), are documented by hand in impl/std/builtins.md and shown here as built in. §21 says which module to look in; spec/21 is the normative text.

std::core, std::collections, std::text, std::io, std::fs, std::env, std::memory, std::sync, std::random, std::math, std::stats, std::time, std::process, std::net, std::crypto::digest, std::crypto::kdf, std::crypto::aead, std::crypto::pk, std::x509, std::tls, std::http, std::http::client, std::http::server, std::database, std::database::postgres, std::encoding::json, std::encoding::hex, std::encoding::base64, std::encoding::toml, std::compress, std::ffi

std::core impl/std/core.cb

Option enum

A value that may be absent: Some(T) holds one, None holds nothing.

In std after import std;, unqualified, as are its variants.

Option::unwrap_or fn

The value in o, or d when o is None.

An unused d is destroyed at the call's end.

Option::ok_or fn

o as a Result: Ok of its value, or Err(e) when o is None, so ? applies.

e is evaluated before the call; unused, it ends with the statement.

Option::unwrap fn

The value in o.

Faults (unwrap_failed) when o is None. Option::expect gives the fault a message of your own; Option::unwrap_or gives a default instead.

Option::expect fn

The value in o, faulting with message when there is none.

Faults (unwrap_failed, showing message) when o is None.

Option::is_some fn

Whether o is Some, without consuming it.

Option::is_none fn

Whether o is None, without consuming it.

Result enum

The outcome of an operation that can fail: Ok(T) holds the value, Err(E) the error.

? on a Result returns an Err from the enclosing function. In std after import std;, unqualified, as are its variants.

Result::ok fn

The value in r as an Option: Some of it, or None when r is Err.

The error, if any, is destroyed at the call's end.

Result::unwrap_or fn

The value in r, or d when r is Err.

An unused d or error is destroyed at the call's end.

Result::unwrap fn

The value in r.

Faults (unwrap_failed) when r is Err; the error's payload is destroyed. Result::expect gives the fault a message of your own.

Result::expect fn

The value in r, faulting with message when r is an error.

Faults (unwrap_failed, showing message) when r is Err; the error's payload is destroyed.

Result::is_ok fn

Whether r is Ok, without consuming it.

Result::is_err fn

Whether r is Err, without consuming it.

Result::map_err built in fn

Keeps an Ok as it is and maps an Err through f: match (r) { Ok(v) : Ok(v), Err(e) : Err(f(e)) }. It is the step that turns a library's error into a program's own before ? passes it on. r is consumed; f runs only for an Err.

AllocError struct

The error allocate returns when memory cannot be had; it carries nothing.

swap fn

Exchanges the values behind a and b.

A program cannot move a value out of a place it reaches through a reference, so it cannot exchange two fields of a borrowed struct itself; this does. Nothing is copied or destroyed: a resource is now owned by the place it is in. Each place is written as *a = v would write it: a live reference that conflicts with either one, such as a shared reborrow of *a, makes the exchange fault. For two elements of one Vec or slice, use Vec::swap or slice_swap, which check the bounds and allow i == j.

replace fn

Puts v in *r and returns what was there.

swap with a fresh value. overwrite destroys the old value instead of returning it.

overwrite fn

Puts v in *r and destroys what was there, at the call.

The way to assign over a place that holds a resource, which plain assignment refuses.

assert built in fn

Checks c and, if it is false, faults with diag.assert-failed, reporting the formatted message if one is given (spec/18 §1a, rule.fail.assert, D-0065). The message's arguments are evaluated only when the assertion fails. An assertion is part of the program's meaning: there is no build in which it is left out, and --check sees its format as it sees printf's. The fault unwinds like any other, so destructors run and a supervised task reports it to its parent.

std::collections impl/std/collections.cb

Vec struct

A growable array of T, owning its elements.

v[i] reads or writes element i (index_out_of_bounds past the end), &v[lo..hi] is a slice of it, and foreach visits it by value, &v or &mut v. A reference to an element is stale after a push that reallocates. Dropping a Vec destroys its elements, first to last, then frees its buffer.

Vec::new fn

A new, empty Vec; nothing is allocated until it first grows.

Vec::len fn

The number of elements in v.

Vec::push fn

Appends x to the end of v.

Amortised constant time: when the buffer is full it is reallocated at twice its capacity, and references to elements held across that are stale at their next use. Faults (alloc_failure) when memory runs out.

Vec::pop fn

Removes the last element of v and returns it; None when v is empty.

Vec::index_shared fn

The element at index i of v, as a shared reference; what v[i] reads, so programs write v[i].

Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

Vec::index_exclusive fn

The element at index i of v, as an exclusive reference; what v[i] is when it is written, so programs write v[i].

Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len. A live slice of v holding i conflicts with it.

Vec::reserve fn

Makes room for n more elements: afterwards the capacity is at least len + n.

Grows at most once, to the larger of len + n and twice the capacity, so small reserves in a loop stay amortised; never shrinks and never changes the length or the elements. It changes only how fast a program runs. len + n overflowing is diag.arith-overflow, before anything is allocated.

Vec::drop fn

Destroys every element of self, first to last, then frees the buffer; the destructor run when a Vec goes out of scope, not called by programs.

Vec::sort_by fn

Sorts v by less, which is true when its first argument goes before its second.

Stable: equal elements (neither before the other) keep their order. Each element moves once. less must be a strict weak order (never less(a, a), transitive); with one that is not, the elements end as a permutation of what they were, in an unspecified order. For a key type Vec::sort needs no less.

Vec::sort fn

Sorts v in its elements' own order, keeping equal elements in their order.

T must be a key type: integers by value, false before true, str and String by their bytes (a prefix first), a struct field by field, an enum by the order its variants are declared in, then by payload. Any other T is rejected at compile time; use Vec::sort_by for those.

Vec::binary_search_by fn

Searches v, sorted by less, for key.

Returns Ok(i) with i the first position whose element is equal to key (neither goes before the other), or Err(i) with i the position where key would be inserted to keep v sorted. v must be sorted by the same less, or the result is unspecified.

Vec::binary_search fn

Searches v, sorted in its elements' own order, for key.

T a key type, as for Vec::sort. Ok(i) for the first position holding an element equal to key, otherwise Err(i), the position where key would go.

Vec::clear fn

Removes every element of v, destroying them first to last; the buffer is kept for reuse.

Vec::insert fn

Inserts x at index i, moving the elements from i on up by one.

i may equal len, which appends. Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i > len. Linear in the number of elements after i; no element is copied.

Vec::remove fn

Removes the element at index i and returns it, moving the elements after it down by one.

Keeps the order and takes time linear in the elements after i; Vec::swap_remove takes constant time but does not keep the order. Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

Vec::swap_remove fn

Removes the element at index i and returns it, moving the last element into its place.

Constant time, but the order is not kept; Vec::remove keeps it. Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

Vec::clone fn

A new Vec holding a copy of each element of v, in order.

T must be clone (owning nothing); for other element types use Vec::clone_by.

Vec::from_slice fn

A new Vec holding a copy of each element of s, in order.

T must be clone. The buffer is allocated once, at the slice's length.

Vec::truncate fn

Keeps the first n elements of v and destroys the rest, last first.

n at or beyond the length leaves v unchanged.

Vec::clone_by fn

A new Vec holding copy(&x) for each element x of v, in order.

For element types that are not clone; copy makes each new element.

Vec::filled fn

A new Vec of n copies of x.

T must be clone; Vec::from_fn builds elements that are not.

Vec::from_raw fn

n elements of plain data copied from C memory into a Vec: a buffer a C caller owns, taken as a value the checks then cover (D-0257). Called inside unsafe { } ([Trusted-Call]): the caller vouches that the n elements at p are readable and stay put for the call.

Vec::from_c_bytes fn

A copy of the bytes C's text at p holds, up to and without its NUL.

Called only inside unsafe: p must point at readable bytes ending in a NUL, as a C function's char * result does. A null p faults (null_pointer); test with is_null first when C may return NULL. String::from_c also checks that the bytes are UTF-8.

Vec::from_fn fn

A new Vec of f(0), f(1), …, f(n - 1), called in that order.

Works for any T, including resources.

Vec::append fn

Moves every element of b onto the end of a, in order; b is consumed.

Vec::extend_from fn

Appends a copy of each element of s to the end of a, in order.

T must be clone. A slice of a itself is rejected (diag.aliasing-conflict).

Vec::position fn

The index of the first element for which p returns true; None when there is none.

p is called in index order and not past the first hit. Vec::index_of looks for an equal element.

Vec::index_of fn

The index of the first element equal to *x; None when there is none.

Vec::contains fn

Whether v has an element equal to *x.

Vec::reverse fn

Reverses the order of the elements of v in place; nothing is copied or destroyed.

Vec::retain fn

Keeps the elements for which keep returns true, in their order, and destroys the rest.

keep is called once per element, in index order, before any element is destroyed. The kept elements are moved down, not copied; the removed ones are destroyed last first.

Vec::dedup fn

Removes every element equal to the one kept before it, keeping the first of each run.

Only adjacent duplicates are removed, so a sorted Vec is left with one of each value. The removed elements are destroyed.

Vec::swap fn

Exchanges elements i and j of v; nothing happens when i == j.

Use it rather than swap(&mut v[i], &mut v[j]), which is two exclusive borrows of one place when i == j. Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when either index is >= len.

Vec::push_le fn

Appends the sizeof<T>() bytes of x to out, least significant byte first (little-endian).

A signed x is written as its two's-complement image. read_le reads it back.

Vec::push_be fn

Appends the sizeof<T>() bytes of x to out, most significant byte first (big-endian, network order).

A signed x is written as its two's-complement image. read_be reads it back.

HashMap struct

A hash table mapping keys of type K to values of type V, kept in insertion order.

K must be a key type: an integer type, bool, str or String, or a struct or enum built only of key types (not f32/f64, not references). Entry i (key_at, value_at) is in insertion order, and foreach (k, v in m) visits the entries in that order; the order depends only on the calls, never on hash values. Replacing a value keeps its entry's place. Lookups borrow the key, so they copy nothing; for a HashMap<String, V> the _str functions look up by a str without making a String. The map owns its keys and values and destroys them with itself.

HashMap::new fn

A new, empty map.

HashMap::clone fn

A new map holding copies of the keys and values of m, in the same insertion order.

HashMap::clear fn

Removes every entry of m, destroying its values and then its keys, each first to last.

HashMap::len fn

The number of entries in m.

HashMap::key_at fn

The key of entry i, in insertion order.

Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

HashMap::value_at fn

The value of entry i, in insertion order.

Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

HashMap::insert fn

Adds key k with value v; returns the old value if k was already present, otherwise None.

A present key keeps its entry's place and its stored key; the k passed in is destroyed.

HashMap::entry fn

The value for k, as an exclusive reference, adding k with the value fresh first if it is absent.

If k is present, k and fresh are not needed and are destroyed. The usual way to count or to collect into a map: *HashMap::entry(&mut m, k, 0) += 1;.

HashMap::get fn

The value for k, as a shared reference; None when k is absent.

HashMap::get_mut fn

The value for k, as an exclusive reference; None when k is absent.

HashMap::contains fn

Whether m has an entry for k.

HashMap::swap_remove fn

Removes k and returns its value, in constant time; None when k is absent.

The last entry moves into the removed one's place, so the insertion order is not kept; HashMap::remove keeps it. The removed key is destroyed.

HashMap::remove fn

Removes k and returns its value; None when k is absent.

The other entries keep their order. Takes time in proportion to the size of the map; HashMap::swap_remove takes constant time but does not keep the order. The removed key is destroyed.

HashMap::get_str fn

The value for the key k in a String-keyed map, as a shared reference; None when it is absent.

Looks the key up by its bytes without making a String, so a literal key costs nothing.

HashMap::get_mut_str fn

The value for the key k in a String-keyed map, as an exclusive reference; None when it is absent.

No String is made.

HashMap::contains_str fn

Whether a String-keyed map has an entry for the key k; no String is made.

HashMap::remove_str fn

Removes the key k from a String-keyed map and returns its value; None when it is absent.

As HashMap::remove: the other entries keep their order. No String is made for the lookup.

HashSet struct

A set of keys of type K, kept in insertion order.

K is a key type, as for HashMap. Key i (key_at) is in insertion order, and foreach (k in s) visits the keys in that order. The set owns its keys and destroys them with itself.

HashSet::new fn

A new, empty set.

HashSet::len fn

The number of keys in s.

HashSet::insert fn

Adds k to s; returns true if it was not already present.

A key already present keeps its place, and the k passed in is destroyed.

HashSet::clone fn

A new set holding copies of the keys of s, in the same order.

HashSet::union fn

A new set of the keys in a or b: a's keys in a's order, then b's keys not in a, in b's order.

The keys are copied with clone; a and b are left as they are.

HashSet::intersection fn

A new set of the keys of a that are also in b, in a's order.

The keys are copied with clone; a and b are left as they are.

HashSet::difference fn

A new set of the keys of a that are not in b, in a's order.

The keys are copied with clone; a and b are left as they are.

HashSet::contains fn

Whether s holds k.

HashSet::swap_remove fn

Removes k from s in constant time; returns true if it was present.

As HashMap::swap_remove, the last key takes k's place, so the order is not kept; HashSet::remove keeps it.

HashSet::remove fn

Removes k from s, keeping the order of the other keys; returns true if it was present.

Takes time in proportion to the size of the set; HashSet::swap_remove is constant time.

HashSet::contains_str fn

Whether a set of Strings holds the text k; no String is made.

HashSet::remove_str fn

Removes the text k from a set of Strings, keeping the order of the others; returns true if it was present.

HashSet::key_at fn

Key i of s, in insertion order.

Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= len.

HashSet::clear fn

Removes every key of s, destroying them, as HashMap::clear does.

Queue struct

A double-ended queue: elements are added and taken at either end in amortised constant time.

The queue owns its elements; dropping it destroys them front to back. There is no positional access, no foreach, no clone and no reserve; a Vec serves those needs.

Queue::new fn

A new, empty queue.

Queue::len fn

The number of elements in q.

Queue::push_back fn

Adds x at the back of q.

Queue::push_front fn

Adds x at the front of q.

Queue::pop_front fn

Removes the front element of q and returns it; None when q is empty.

Queue::pop_back fn

Removes the back element of q and returns it; None when q is empty.

Queue::front fn

The front element of q, as a shared reference; None when q is empty.

The reference borrows the queue, which cannot change while it is in use.

Queue::back fn

The back element of q, as a shared reference; None when q is empty.

The reference borrows the queue, which cannot change while it is in use.

Queue::clear fn

Removes every element of q, destroying them front to back; the buffers are kept.

Queue::drop fn

Destroys the elements of self, front to back; the destructor run when a Queue goes out of scope, not called by programs.

PriorityQueue struct

A priority queue: it gives its elements back least first, in an order fixed when it is made.

PriorityQueue::new uses the key types' own order, PriorityQueue::new_by the caller's less. Elements the order calls equal come out first in, first out. A binary heap: push and pop take time in proportion to the logarithm of the length. The queue owns its elements. There is no peek_mut (pop, change and push instead), no foreach, no clone and no reserve.

PriorityQueue::new fn

A new, empty priority queue in the key types' own order, smallest first (as Vec::sort orders).

T must be a key type; for any other T use PriorityQueue::new_by.

PriorityQueue::new_by fn

With n elements, each part has n / parts elements and the first n % parts parts one more; some are empty when parts > n. The result is empty when parts is 0. The parts are disjoint, so each can be given to a thread of its own (spawn(work, part)) and written there without a lock; the borrow of s ends when the last part ends.

std::io impl/std/io.cb

File::printf built in fn

Writes the formatted text to the open file *f, as printf would to standard output (D-0059); the format is checked when the program is compiled. A write that fails is the Err, as for File::write. File itself is std::fs's type; this function is registered with the printf family in std::io, and import std; brings in both.

flush_stdout fn

Writes out what standard output still holds in its buffer.

Standard output is buffered; standard error is not. Reading standard input, writing to standard error, exit and the program's end write the buffer out themselves, so this is needed only when standard output is a pipe or a file that someone watches while the program runs (progress, a log), and before handing over to C code that writes through stdio.

read_line fn

The next line of standard input, without its line ending, or Ok(None) at the end of the input.

  • A line is every byte up to the next \n, which is consumed and not included; a \r just before it is consumed with it, so a Windows line ending reads as a Unix one. A last line with no \n is still a line, and keeps a final \r.
  • Ok(None) when the input ended before the line's first byte, and on every call after that.
  • Err(FileError::Utf8(e)) when the line is not UTF-8, e.offset counted within the line; the line is consumed, so the next call reads the one after it.
  • Err(FileError::Io) when standard input cannot be read; the bytes of the line read so far are lost.

read_all_bytes fn

The rest of standard input, as bytes; empty when the input has already ended.

Err(FileError::Io) when standard input cannot be read. read_all takes it as text.

read_all fn

The rest of standard input, as text.

Err(FileError::Utf8(e)) when it is not UTF-8, and Err(FileError::Io) when it cannot be read; read_all_bytes takes it as bytes.

printf built in fn

Writes the arguments to standard output as the format f says (spec/21 §2f, rule.stdlib.format). f is a string literal, so the format and the arguments are checked when the program is compiled and nothing about it can fail at run time. The conversions are C's: %d for any integer type (there is no %ld), %u, %x, %X, %o, %b (binary) for an integer's bits in its own width, %f, %e, %g for f32 and f64, %s for a str, a ref<String, shared> or a bool, and %v for any printable value or enum "as CobaltC writes it" (an enum's variant name; a float that reads back as the same value). Width and precision may be *, taking the next argument (a usize). A reference to a number, a bool or a str prints as what it refers to, so foreach (x in &v) { printf("%d\n", x); } prints the elements. Output is buffered (D-0178) and written out when the buffer fills, at flush_stdout(), and when the program ends.

eprintf built in fn

Writes the arguments to standard error as the format f says, with printf's conversions. For messages that are not the program's output: errors, warnings, progress. Standard error is written at once, with nothing held back, so its text and standard output's interleave in the order the calls ran (after a flush_stdout(), exactly).

stdout_write extern fn

Writes the len bytes at buf to standard output: the primitive under printf.

Called inside unsafe, with buf pointing at len readable bytes; its result is a claim like any extern's. What it writes goes through the same buffer as printf (flush_stdout). Programs write with printf.

stdin_read extern fn

Reads up to len bytes of standard input into buf: the primitive under read_all_bytes.

Called inside unsafe, with buf pointing at len writable bytes. Its result, a claim like any extern's, is the number of bytes read: 0 at the end of the input, negative when the input cannot be read. Programs read with read_line, read_all or read_all_bytes.

FileError enum

The error of every input and output operation of std, for files and standard input alike.

  • NotFound: no such file, or a directory on the path does not exist.
  • Denied: the environment refuses the operation.
  • Io: any other failure (the path names a directory, a device error, …).
  • Utf8(e): the bytes read are not UTF-8; e gives the offset of the first byte that is not.

FileError::text fn

The error as a short phrase for a person (not found, permission denied).

File struct

An open file, read and written in order from a position that seek moves.

Every File comes from File::open, create, append, open_rw or create_new. Positions are u64, so a file larger than the address space is still addressed. Reading and writing are buffered; the bytes written reach the file no later than the next operation on it, any other file-system operation of the program, the start of a child process, or the program's end.

Destroying a File closes it without making it durable and without reporting a failure; a program that must know its bytes were stored calls File::close.

File::open fn

Opens the existing file at path for reading, at position 0.

Err(NotFound) when there is no such file; Err(Denied) when the environment refuses; Err(Io) for any other failure (the path names a directory).

File::create fn

Opens the file at path for writing from empty, creating it or discarding its contents.

Err(NotFound) when a directory on the path does not exist; Err(Denied), Err(Io) as File::open's. Use File::create_new when an existing file must not be overwritten.

File::append fn

Opens the file at path for writing at its end, creating it if it does not exist.

Every write lands at the end of the file.

File::open_rw fn

Opens the file at path for reading and writing, creating it if it does not exist, its contents kept.

The position starts at 0; a write lands at the position reading has reached.

File::read fn

Appends up to max bytes from the file's position to the end of buf and returns how many.

At most a MiB is read at a time, whatever max is; fewer bytes come only at the end of the file, and Ok(0) (for a max above 0) means the end. Err(Io) on a file opened only for writing.

File::read_to_end fn

Appends the rest of the file, from its position, to the end of buf and returns how many bytes.

File::read_line fn

The next line of the file, without its final '\n' or one '\r' just before it.

Ok(None) at the end of the file. A last line with no '\n' is still a line. Err(Utf8(e)) when the line is not UTF-8, e's offset counted from the line's start; Err(Io) on a file opened only for writing. Lines end as read_line on standard input ends them.

File::write fn

Writes all of data at the file's position, or at its end for a file opened by File::append.

The file grows as needed and the position moves past the bytes written. Writes are buffered (see File); a failure the environment reports late is reported by the file's next operation. Err(Io) on a file opened only for reading.

File::write_text fn

Writes the bytes of text at the file's position, as File::write does.

File::seek fn

Moves the file's position to byte pos from the start.

A position beyond the end is allowed: reading there gives 0 bytes, and writing there extends the file.

File::len fn

The file's length in bytes.

File::create_new fn

Opens a new file at path for writing, only if nothing is there yet.

Ok(None) when a file or a directory of that name already exists, and nothing is changed, so of two programs that race to make the same file exactly one wins: a lock file, a pid file, a file that must never be overwritten. Err(NotFound) when a directory above path does not exist; other errors as File::create's.

File::flush fn

Makes everything written to the file so far durable.

The bytes are handed to the operating system and by it to the device, and from then on survive a crash or a power loss; the write-then-rename pattern flushes before the rename. Err(Io) on a file open only for reading, or when the device fails.

File::position fn

The byte the next read or write starts at, counted from the start of the file.

It is 0 when the file is opened (for File::append, the length once something is written) and is moved by every read, read_line, write and seek.

File::close fn

Closes the file, first making a file open for writing durable, and reports any failure.

Err(e) when the environment reports a failure, including one for bytes written earlier; the file is closed all the same. Destroying a File closes it too, but reports nothing.

File::drop fn

Closes an open file when its File is destroyed, without making it durable or reporting a failure.

The destructor; programs do not call it, and call File::close to learn whether the bytes were stored.

PathKind enum

What a path names, as path_kind and file_info report it.

  • Dir: a directory.
  • Other: something else, such as a device or a socket.

What file_info reports of a path.

The whole contents of the file at path, as text.

read_bytes fn

The whole contents of the file at path, as bytes.

The errors are File::open's and File::read_to_end's. Use read_file for text.

write_bytes fn

Makes the file at path hold exactly data, creating it or replacing its contents.

The errors are File::create's and File::write's. Use write_file for text.

Makes the directory path, whose parent must exist.

Ok(true) when it was made; Ok(false) when a directory was already there, so it is safe to call again. Err(NotFound) when the parent does not exist; Err(Io) when something that is not a directory is at path. Use make_dir_all to make the missing parents too.

Err(NotFound) when there is none.

remove_dir fn

Removes the empty directory at path.

Err(Io) when it is not empty; Err(NotFound) when there is none. Use remove_dir_all to remove a directory and everything in it.

rename fn

Renames (moves) what is at from to to, replacing a file at to.

list_dir fn

The names of the entries of the directory path, sorted by their bytes.

The names are entry names, not paths (join them to path with path_join), and never . or ... Err(Utf8(e)) for a name that is not UTF-8.

path_kind fn

What path names: a file and its length, a directory, or something else.

A symbolic link is followed. Err(NotFound) when nothing is at path.

path_join fn

The path base followed by tail, with the platform's separator between them.

No separator is added after one base already ends with. An absolute tail is returned alone. Reads the text only, never the file system.

The path p without its last part.

None for a root or the empty path; the empty path for a single relative name. Reads the text only, never the file system; the grammar is the platform's (\ also separates parts on Windows).

path_file_name fn

The last part of the path p.

None when the last part is .., or when there is none (/, the empty path). Reads the text only.

path_stem fn

The file name of p without its extension (archive.tar of archive.tar.gz).

A name whose only dot is its first byte has no extension, so its stem is the whole name (.bashrc). Reads the text only.

path_extension fn

The extension of the file name of p, without its dot (gz of archive.tar.gz).

None when there is none: a name with no dot, or whose only dot is its first byte. Reads the text only.

path_is_absolute fn

Whether p names a place without the working directory.

By the platform's grammar: a leading / on Unix; C:\ or \\server\share\ on Windows. Reads the text only.

path_normalize fn

The path p with every . part removed and every x/.. (x a name) resolved.

By the text alone: a link is not followed, so the result can name another place than p when x is a link. A leading .. stays, /.. is /, and a path with no part left is .. Use path_canonical to ask the file system.

path_canonical fn

The absolute path the operating system resolves p to, with every link followed.

p must exist: Err(NotFound) when nothing is at p; Err(Utf8(e)) when the result is not UTF-8.

file_info fn

The kind, length, modification time and read-only state of what is at path.

A symbolic link is followed, as path_kind follows it. Err(NotFound) when nothing is at path.

copy_file fn

Copies the file from to to, replacing a file there, and returns the number of bytes copied.

copy_permissions fn

Gives what is at to the permissions of what is at from: on Unix the mode bits, on Windows the read-only flag.

For the write-then-rename pattern: a file written beside the original and renamed over it keeps the original's permissions only when they are copied to it before the rename. Err(NotFound) when nothing is at from or at to.

make_dir_all fn

Makes the directory path and every missing directory above it.

Ok(()) when they are all there already.

remove_dir_all fn

Removes the directory path and everything in it.

Err(NotFound) when nothing is at path.

std::env impl/std/env.cb

Args struct

The program's arguments, read as options and positional arguments.

Each Args::flag, Args::option or Args::options call names an option, takes its occurrences from the arguments and adds a line to Args::help; Args::finish then gives the arguments left and refuses any option nobody declared. --name, --name=value, --name value, -s and -s value are read; -- ends the options, and a lone - is an argument.

Args::new fn

The program's arguments, from arg(0) on, with the usage line that Args::help shows.

The usage line is the text after Usage: , such as prog [options] FILE.

Err(e) for the first argument that is not UTF-8.

Args::from fn

The arguments items, read as Args::new reads the program's own.

For arguments that come from elsewhere, or a test.

Args::flag fn

Whether --name or -short is among the arguments before --.

short is one letter, or "" for none; help is the option's line in Args::help. Every occurrence is taken, so Args::finish does not see it.

Args::options fn

Every value given for the option --name or -short, in order.

A value is given as --name=value, --name value or -s value; each is taken, the value with it. value_name names the value in Args::help (FILE). A --name or -s that is the last argument, just before --, or followed by an argument an earlier declaration took (a flag's -v), has no value and is left for Args::finish to refuse.

Args::option fn

The value of the option --name or -short, the last one when it is given more than once.

None when it is not given. Takes its arguments as Args::options does.

Args::finish fn

The arguments no declaration took, in order, every argument after -- among them.

Err(message) for the first argument before -- that starts with - and is not a lone -: unknown option --x, or missing a value for --x for a declared option given without its value. The message is for the program to print, usually followed by Args::help.

Args::help fn

The usage line and one aligned line per option declared so far, ready to print.

arg_count fn

The number of the program's arguments, not counting the program's own name.

arg fn

Argument i of the program, counted from 0 for the first after the program's own name.

Err(e) when the argument is not UTF-8, e.offset being the bad byte's offset within it; use arg_bytes for such an argument. Faults (index_out_of_bounds) when i >= arg_count().

env_var fn

The value of the environment variable name.

Ok(None) when it is not set; Err(e) when its value is not UTF-8, e giving the offset of the first byte that is not.

current_dir fn

The working directory, against which a relative path is resolved.

Err(Utf8(e)) when its name is not UTF-8.

set_current_dir fn

Makes path the working directory, against which relative paths are resolved from now on.

The change is seen by every thread of the program.

temp_dir fn

The operating system's directory for temporary files.

A byte sequence in it that is not UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD.

home_dir fn

The user's home directory: the variable HOME, or USERPROFILE on Windows.

None when it is not set. A byte sequence that is not UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD.

current_exe fn

The path of the running program's own executable, absolute and with links followed.

A program finds the files installed beside it from here. Err(Utf8(e)) when the path is not UTF-8; Err(Io) when the operating system cannot say.

hostname fn

The machine's host name, as the operating system knows it.

What a log line or a service's registration names the machine by. Err(Utf8(e)) when it is not UTF-8; Err(Io) when the operating system cannot say.

arg_bytes extern fn

Copies at most len bytes of argument i to buf and returns the argument's whole length.

Returns -1, storing nothing, when there is no argument i; a call with len 0 only asks whether argument i exists and how long it is. Called inside unsafe: [buf, buf + len) must be storage outside every live object. For an argument's bytes whatever they are; arg is the safe way to read one.

std::memory impl/std/memory.cb

Rc struct

A reference-counted handle to a value on the heap that several owners share.

Each Rc is one strong handle; the value is destroyed when the last strong handle is, and the memory is freed once no Weak handle remains either. The value is reached only as a shared reference (Rc::get), so changing it needs a mutex inside. A cycle of Rcs is never freed: a parent pointer, a cache or an observer list holds a Weak instead. Rc is not thread-safe (the count is not synchronised); share across threads with ref<mutex<T>, shared>.

Rc::new fn

A new Rc holding v, the only strong handle to it.

Allocates; faults (alloc_failure) when memory cannot be had.

Rc::clone fn

A second strong handle to the value r holds; nothing is copied.

What clone(&r) calls for an Rc. A reference into the value from Rc::get may stay live across it.

Rc::get fn

The value r holds, as a shared reference.

Rc::drop fn

Ends one strong handle; run when an Rc is destroyed, so programs write drop(r) or let it go.

When this was the last strong handle the value is destroyed now, and with no Weak handle left the memory is freed too.

Rc::downgrade fn

A Weak handle to the value r holds.

Weak struct

A handle to an Rc's value that does not keep the value alive.

It keeps only the memory: once the last Rc ends, the value is gone and Weak::upgrade gives None. Dropping the last handle of either kind frees the memory.

Weak::upgrade fn

A new strong handle to the value, or None when the value has ended.

The value never comes back once ended: after the last Rc is destroyed every upgrade gives None.

Weak::clone fn

A second Weak handle to the same value; what clone(&w) calls for a Weak.

Weak::drop fn

Ends one weak handle; run when a Weak is destroyed.

When no strong or weak handle remains, the memory is freed.

Arc struct

A reference-counted handle to a value that several threads share.

Rc for threads: each Arc is one strong handle, and handles may be cloned into other threads, moved and dropped there, so a thread owns its share of the value and may outlive the frame that made it, which a reference to the value does not allow. The counts are atomic, so clones and drops from several threads at once lose nothing; the value is destroyed, once, by whichever handle ends last. It is reached only as a shared reference (Arc::get), so changing it needs a mutex or an Atomic inside. An ArcWeak (Arc::downgrade) keeps the box but not the value, for a parent pointer or a cache.

Arc::new fn

A new Arc holding v, the only strong handle to it.

Allocates; faults (alloc_failure) when memory cannot be had.

Arc::clone fn

A second strong handle to the value a holds; nothing is copied.

What clone(&a) calls for an Arc. The new handle may go to another thread.

Arc::get fn

The value a holds, as a shared reference.

Arc::drop fn

Ends one strong handle; run when an Arc is destroyed, so programs write drop(a) or let it go.

When this was the last strong handle, on whichever thread, the value is destroyed now, and with no ArcWeak handle left the memory is freed too.

Arc::downgrade fn

An ArcWeak handle to the value a holds.

ArcWeak struct

A handle that does not keep the value alive.

As Weak is to Rc: it keeps only the memory. Once the last Arc ends, the value is gone and ArcWeak::upgrade gives None. Dropping the last handle of either kind frees the memory.

ArcWeak::upgrade fn

A new strong handle to the value, or None when the value has ended.

The value never comes back once ended: after the last Arc is destroyed every upgrade gives None.

ArcWeak::clone fn

A second ArcWeak handle to the same value; what clone(&w) calls for an ArcWeak.

ArcWeak::drop fn

Ends one weak handle; run when an ArcWeak is destroyed.

When no strong or weak handle remains, the memory is freed.

Box struct

A value on the heap with one owner.

It gives recursive types their indirection (struct Node { i32 v; Option<Box<Node>> next; }) and moves a large value as a pointer. A Box is a resource: it moves, and destroying it destroys the value and frees the memory. It allocates sizeof<T>() bytes, or one for a zero-sized T.

Box::new fn

A new Box holding v.

Allocates; faults (alloc_failure) when memory cannot be had.

Box::get fn

The value in b, as a shared reference.

Box::get_mut fn

The value in b, as an exclusive reference.

Needs an exclusive borrow of the Box, as changing any value does.

Box::clone fn

A new Box holding a copy of the value in b; what clone(&b) calls for a Box.

Box::into_inner fn

The value in b, moved out; the Box's memory is freed.

Faults if another thread holds an exclusive path to the value.

Box::drop fn

Destroys the value and frees the memory; run when a Box is destroyed.

std::sync impl/std/sync.cb

Channel struct

A bounded first-in, first-out queue of values between threads.

Shared by reference, as a mutex is: every thread works on it through ref<Channel<T>, shared>. send waits while it is full and recv while it is empty; after close, send gives its value back and recv drains what is left, then gives None. Destroying the channel destroys the values still in it, oldest first.

Channel::new fn

An empty open channel holding at most cap values.

Faults (channel_zero_capacity) when cap is 0; 1 makes a hand-over.

Channel::send fn

Puts v at the back of ch, waiting while the channel is full.

Err(v), the value handed back, once the channel is closed. Exclusive references inside v are lent to the receiving thread: the sender's own copies of them clash with them while they live.

Channel::recv fn

Takes the value at the front of ch, waiting while the channel is empty.

None once the channel is closed and empty.

Channel::try_recv fn

Takes the value at the front of ch if one is waiting, without waiting.

Ok(Some(v)) with the value; Ok(None) when the channel is empty; Err(()) once it is closed and empty, so a loop that also polls something else (a socket, interrupt_requested) knows when the senders are done.

Channel::recv_timeout_ms fn

Takes the value at the front of ch, waiting at most ms milliseconds for one.

Ok(Some(v)) with the value; Ok(None) when none arrived in time; Err(()) when the channel is closed and empty. The wait is a poll (every millisecond at first, then every five), so it ends at most a few milliseconds late.

Channel::close fn

Marks ch as taking no more values.

send fails from then on, and recv gives None once the values already in it are taken. Waiting senders and receivers wake. Closing a closed channel does nothing.

Channel::drop fn

Destroys the values still in the channel, oldest first; run when a Channel is destroyed.

ThreadFailure struct

A spawned thread's fault, contained and handed over by try_join instead of raised again.

Its text is kept by the runtime until the program ends.

ThreadFailure::text fn

The failure's report, as the program would have printed it had nothing taken the failure.

As a fault's report on standard error: its first line names the diagnostic, its second the location.

ThreadFailure::diagnostic fn

The name of the failure's diagnostic alone, such as diag.index-out-of-bounds or diag.thread-cancelled.

ThreadFailure::is_cancelled fn

Whether the thread ended because it was cancelled, rather than by a fault of its own.

Atomic struct

An integer that threads share and change without a lock.

Shared by reference, as a mutex is: every operation takes ref<Atomic<T>, shared>, and each one is indivisible and sequentially consistent, so all threads see all operations on all atomics in one order. T is an integer type of at most 64 bits. For a counter, a flag (an Atomic<u8>), a sequence number or a maximum kept by several threads; state of more than one integer belongs in a mutex.

Atomic::new fn

A new atomic holding v.

T is an integer type of at most 64 bits: Atomic<u128> is rejected when the program is checked.

Atomic::load fn

The value a holds.

Atomic::store fn

Replaces the value a holds with v.

Atomic::swap fn

Replaces the value a holds with v, giving the value it held.

Atomic::compare_exchange fn

Replaces the value with new if it is expected, as one step.

Ok(expected) when it was replaced; Err(current) with the value found when it was not, and then nothing changed. The step under a lock-free update: read, compute, and try again from current when another thread got there first.

Atomic::fetch_add fn

Adds n to the value a holds, giving the value it held.

Faults (arith_overflow) when the sum does not fit T, as + does, and then the value is unchanged. fetch_add_wrapping wraps instead.

Atomic::fetch_sub fn

Subtracts n from the value a holds, giving the value it held.

Faults (arith_overflow) when the difference does not fit T, as - does, and then the value is unchanged. fetch_sub_wrapping wraps instead.

Atomic::fetch_add_wrapping fn

Adds n to the value a holds modulo 2 to the width of T, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_sub_wrapping fn

Subtracts n from the value a holds modulo 2 to the width of T, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_and fn

Replaces the value a holds with its bitwise and with n, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_or fn

Replaces the value a holds with its bitwise or with n, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_xor fn

Replaces the value a holds with its bitwise exclusive or with n, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_max fn

Replaces the value a holds with the larger of it and v, giving the value it held.

A maximum kept by several threads: a high-water mark, the latest timestamp seen.

Atomic::fetch_min fn

Replaces the value a holds with the smaller of it and v, giving the value it held.

Atomic::fetch_update fn

Replaces the value a holds with f of it, retrying when another thread changed it meanwhile.

f is called with the value found and gives Some(new) to store or None to leave it. Ok(previous) when new was stored, Err(previous) when f gave None. f may be called more than once, so it should compute only from its argument.

Atomic::wait fn

Blocks while a holds expected, until another thread changes it and calls notify_one or notify_all.

Returns at once if a does not hold expected, and otherwise only after it has seen another value, so a wake-up with the value unchanged waits again. The thread that changes the value calls notify_one or notify_all after the change. A wait no thread can end faults (deadlock).

Atomic::notify_one fn

Wakes at least one thread waiting in Atomic::wait on a, if any waits.

Atomic::notify_all fn

Wakes every thread waiting in Atomic::wait on a.

AtomicBool struct

A bool that threads share and change without a lock.

As Atomic, over a byte that holds 0 or 1: every operation takes ref<AtomicBool, shared> and is indivisible and sequentially consistent. For a stop flag, a "ready" flag, or a once-only claim (swap(&f, true) gives false to exactly one thread).

AtomicBool::new fn

A new atomic bool holding v.

AtomicBool::load fn

The value f holds.

AtomicBool::store fn

Replaces the value f holds with v.

AtomicBool::swap fn

Replaces the value f holds with v, giving the value it held.

AtomicBool::compare_exchange fn

Replaces the value with new if it is expected, as one step: Ok(expected), or Err(current).

AtomicBool::fetch_and fn

Replaces the value f holds with its and with v, giving the value it held.

AtomicBool::fetch_or fn

Replaces the value f holds with its or with v, giving the value it held.

AtomicBool::fetch_xor fn

Replaces the value f holds with its exclusive or with v, giving the value it held.

AtomicBool::wait fn

Blocks while f holds expected, as Atomic::wait.

AtomicBool::notify_one fn

Wakes at least one thread waiting in AtomicBool::wait on f, if any waits.

AtomicBool::notify_all fn

Wakes every thread waiting in AtomicBool::wait on f.

AtomicPtr struct

A raw pointer that threads share and change without a lock.

As Atomic: shared by reference, every operation indivisible and sequentially consistent. Taking and storing addresses is safe; reading or writing through one is unsafe, as for any rawptr. For lock-free lists and stacks whose nodes come from allocate.

AtomicPtr::new fn

A new atomic pointer holding p; null_rawptr<T>() for none.

AtomicPtr::load fn

The address a holds.

AtomicPtr::store fn

Replaces the address a holds with p.

AtomicPtr::swap fn

Replaces the address a holds with p, giving the address it held.

AtomicPtr::compare_exchange fn

Replaces the address with new if it is expected, as one step: Ok(expected), or Err(current).

Barrier struct

A meeting point for a fixed number of threads.

Shared by reference, as a mutex is. Barrier::wait blocks until parties threads have called it, then releases them all together and is ready for the next round: the phases of a parallel algorithm, where every thread must finish one before any starts the next.

Barrier::new fn

A barrier for parties threads.

Faults (barrier_zero_parties) when parties is 0.

Barrier::wait fn

Waits until parties threads have called it, then lets them all go on.

true for the last thread to arrive, the one that released the others, and false for the rest, so one thread of each round can do something once. A wait that fewer threads than parties can ever reach faults (deadlock).

Semaphore struct

A count of permits that threads take and give back.

Shared by reference, as a mutex is. acquire takes one permit, waiting while there is none; release gives one back, or adds one. It bounds how many threads do something at once (connections open, workers busy); made with 0 permits, it hands events from one thread to another, each release letting one acquire through.

Semaphore::new fn

A semaphore with permits permits; 0 is allowed.

Semaphore::acquire fn

Takes one permit, waiting while there is none.

Permits are not handed out in arrival order. A wait no thread can end faults (deadlock).

Semaphore::try_acquire fn

Takes one permit if one is free, without waiting: true when it did.

Semaphore::release fn

Gives one permit back, or adds one; a thread waiting in acquire wakes.

Faults (arith_overflow) when the permits would exceed what usize counts.

Semaphore::available fn

How many permits are free now: a snapshot another thread may change at once.

Once struct

Something done once, by whichever thread gets there first.

Shared by reference, as a mutex is. Once::call(&o, f) runs f the first time any thread calls it; every other call, on any thread, returns once that run has finished, without running f: initialising what several threads share, lazily and exactly once. Should f fault, the Once is as before, and the next caller runs f afresh.

Once::new fn

A Once whose f has not run.

Once::call fn

Runs f if no call has run it yet; otherwise waits until the call that is running it has finished.

f runs on the calling thread. After call returns, on any thread, f has run to its end exactly once (unless it faulted, and then the next caller runs it again).

Once::is_done fn

Whether f has run to its end.

cpu_count fn

How many threads the machine runs at once, at least 1: the size of a worker pool.

The processors, or what this program may use of them.

try_join fn

Waits for the thread h and gives its result, or its failure as a value instead of raising it again.

Ok of the thread's result; Err(ThreadFailure) when the thread faulted or was cancelled, and the failure is then taken, so nothing is raised. How a supervisor keeps going when a worker has a bug; join raises the failure instead.

is_finished fn

Whether the thread h has ended, its result or failure waiting for join or try_join.

Never waits and takes nothing: how a supervisor finds which of its threads to take.

atomic_fence fn

A full memory fence: every memory access before it, in this thread, is ordered before every one after it, as seen by any other thread or device.

CobaltC's own operations are already sequentially consistent, so a program that stays within them never needs this. It is for raw and volatile accesses and C code, which are outside that guarantee: the equivalent of C's atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_seq_cst).

spin_hint fn

Tells the processor that this thread is spinning, waiting for another thread to change something.

The CPU's pause instruction: it saves power and lets the other hardware thread of the core run. Call it in the body of a loop that polls an atomic; Atomic::wait blocks instead, for waits that may be long.

std::random impl/std/random.cb

Rng struct

A general-purpose pseudo-random generator: xoshiro256** seeded through splitmix64.

The same seed gives the same sequence in every implementation, so a run can be reproduced. Not suitable for cryptographic purposes: its state is recoverable from its output, so it must not produce keys, tokens or nonces; use os_random_bytes for those.

Rng::new fn

A generator seeded from seed; equal seeds give equal sequences.

Rng::from_os seeds one unpredictably instead.

Rng::next_u64 fn

The next 64 pseudo-random bits from r.

Rng::below fn

A pseudo-random number from 0 up to, not including, n, each value equally likely.

Unbiased: a draw that would favour some values is rejected and drawn again. Faults (div_by_zero) when n is 0.

Rng::unit_f64 fn

A pseudo-random f64 with 0.0 <= x < 1.0, from the top 53 bits of one draw.

Rng::from_os fn

A generator seeded from the operating system's secure source, so each run draws a different sequence.

The sequence itself is still Rng's, so it is still not for cryptographic purposes.

Rng::shuffle fn

Puts the elements of s in a uniformly random order drawn from r.

Fisher-Yates over Rng::below; elements are exchanged, never copied. The same seed gives the same order in every implementation.

os_random_bytes fn

Fills out with bytes from the operating system's cryptographically secure source.

Suitable for keys, tokens and nonces, and for seeding Rng. Faults (entropy_unavailable) when the system has no such source.

os_random_u64 fn

A u64 from the operating system's cryptographically secure source.

Faults (entropy_unavailable) when the system has no such source.

uuid_v4 fn

A version 4 UUID (RFC 9562) from the operating system's secure source, as 36 lowercase characters.

The form is xxxxxxxx-xxxx-4xxx-yxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx, with y one of 8, 9, a, b. Faults (entropy_unavailable) when the system has no secure source.

std::math impl/std/math.cb

BigUint struct

An unsigned integer of any size, for public-key arithmetic and numbers too large for u128.

Each operation gives the exact integer result. The time an operation takes depends on its operands' values, so a BigUint is for public values only, never a private key or anything secret. It owns its digits, so a program reassigns one with overwrite.

BigUint::zero fn

The number 0.

BigUint::from_u64 fn

The number x.

BigUint::from_bytes_be fn

The number whose big-endian bytes are bytes; leading zero bytes are allowed, and no bytes give 0.

BigUint::to_bytes_be fn

The big-endian bytes of a, with no leading zero byte; none for zero.

BigUint::to_bytes_be_padded gives a fixed width instead.

BigUint::to_bytes_be_padded fn

The big-endian bytes of a in exactly width bytes, zeros in front.

Faults (arith_overflow) when a needs more than width bytes.

BigUint::is_zero fn

Whether a is 0.

BigUint::bit_len fn

The number of bits needed to write a; 0 for zero.

BigUint::bit fn

Whether bit i of a is set, bit 0 being the least significant; false beyond bit_len.

BigUint::eq fn

Whether a and b are the same number.

BigUint::less fn

Whether a is less than b; fits Vec::sort_by.

BigUint::add fn

The sum a + b.

BigUint::sub fn

The difference a - b.

Faults (arith_overflow) when b is greater than a, as for any unsigned subtraction.

BigUint::mul fn

The product a * b.

BigUint::shift_right fn

a divided by 2 to the power k, rounded down.

BigUint::shift_left fn

a times 2 to the power k.

BigUint::div_rem fn

The quotient of a by b, rounded down, and the remainder, together.

Faults (div_by_zero) when b is 0. BigUint::rem gives only the remainder.

BigUint::rem fn

a modulo m.

Faults (div_by_zero) when m is 0.

BigUint::mod_pow fn

base raised to the power exp, modulo m.

By squaring and multiplying, reducing at each step. Faults (div_by_zero) when m is 0; anything modulo 1 is 0.

BigUint::clone fn

A copy of a; what clone(&a) calls for a BigUint.

BigUint::mod_inverse fn

The inverse of a modulo m: the number below m whose product with a is 1 modulo m.

None when a and m share a factor above 1, or when m is below 2. Its time depends on the values, as every BigUint operation's does: for public numbers and one-time blinding factors, not a private key.

BigUint::text fn

a in decimal digits, with no leading zero.

BigUint::parse fn

The number written in decimal digits in text.

Err(Empty) when text is empty; Err(Invalid(i)) at the first byte i that is not a digit (a sign is not accepted).

BigDivision struct

The quotient and remainder that BigUint::div_rem gives.

Taken apart by destructuring: BigDivision { quotient, remainder } = BigUint::div_rem(&a, &b);.

min fn

The smaller of a and b; a when they are equal.

max fn

The larger of a and b; a when they are equal.

abs fn

The magnitude of x.

Checked: faults (arith_overflow) for a signed type's minimum, whose magnitude does not fit. abs(-0.0) is 0.0, and a NaN stays a NaN.

pow fn

base raised to the power exp, by repeated squaring; pow(x, 0) is 1.

Checked: faults (arith_overflow) only when the result does not fit in T. For a floating-point exponent, use powf.

clamp fn

x held within lo ..= hi: lo when x is below it, hi when above, else x.

Faults (assert_failed) when lo is above hi.

is_nan fn

Whether x is a NaN, the one value not equal to itself; false for every integer.

is_finite fn

Whether x is neither a NaN nor an infinity; true for every integer.

gcd fn

The greatest common divisor of a and b, never negative; gcd(0, 0) is 0.

Euclid's algorithm over the magnitudes, so a signed type's minimum faults (arith_overflow) as in abs.

sqrt built in fn

The square root of x, correctly rounded ([Float-Fn], spec/21 §3d, D-0091): every conforming implementation gives the same bits. A NaN for a negative x; -0.0 for -0.0; a NaN in gives a NaN out.

floor built in fn

x rounded to an integral value toward negative infinity, exactly ([Float-Fn]). A NaN or an infinity is returned as it is.

ceil built in fn

x rounded to an integral value toward positive infinity, exactly ([Float-Fn]).

round built in fn

x rounded to the nearest integral value, halfway cases away from zero (2.5 to 3.0, -2.5 to -3.0), exactly ([Float-Fn]). Convert the result with rule.arith.convert when an integer is wanted.

trunc built in fn

x rounded to an integral value toward zero, exactly ([Float-Fn]): the fractional part dropped.

ln built in fn

The natural logarithm of x, within one unit in the last place of the mathematical value ([Float-Transcendental], D-0101): the platform's C library computes it, so coby and cobc agree on one platform and may differ in the last bit between platforms. A NaN for a negative x; negative infinity for ±0.

exp built in fn

e to the power x, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]). Overflows to infinity as IEEE-754 says.

log2 built in fn

The base-2 logarithm of x, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]); a NaN for a negative x, negative infinity for ±0. For an integer's bit length, integer arithmetic is exact and cheaper.

log10 built in fn

The base-10 logarithm of x, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]); a NaN for a negative x, negative infinity for ±0.

sin built in fn

The sine of x, an angle in radians, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]).

cos built in fn

The cosine of x, an angle in radians, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]).

tan built in fn

The tangent of x, an angle in radians, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental]).

asin built in fn

The arc sine of x, in radians in [-π/2, π/2], within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental], D-0181); a NaN for x outside [-1, 1].

acos built in fn

The arc cosine of x, in radians in [0, π], within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental], D-0181); a NaN for x outside [-1, 1].

atan built in fn

The arc tangent of x, in radians in (-π/2, π/2), within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental], D-0181). For an angle from two coordinates use atan2, which knows the quadrant.

atan2 built in fn

The angle of the point (x, y) from the positive x axis, in radians in (-π, π], within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental-2]); C's atan2. Both operands have the same type.

powf built in fn

x to the power y for floating-point operands, within one unit in the last place ([Float-Transcendental-2]); C's pow. For an integer exponent, pow (an ordinary std::math function) is exact and checked for overflow.

std::stats impl/std/stats.cb

Summary struct

What describe gives: the count of the values and their minimum, maximum, mean, population standard deviation and median.

sum fn

The sum of data's values in their own type; 0 for an empty slice.

Added left to right with +, so an integer sum that does not fit in T faults (arith_overflow), as + does. For the sum as an f64 whatever T is, multiply mean by the count.

mean fn

The arithmetic mean of data's values; None for an empty slice.

Each value is converted to f64 with to_float and the values added left to right, then divided by the count. A NaN among the values makes the mean a NaN.

variance fn

The population variance of data's values, the mean of the squared deviations from their mean; None for an empty slice.

Two passes: the mean first, then the sum of (x - mean)² left to right, divided by the count. For the variance of a sample drawn from a larger population, use sample_variance.

stddev fn

The population standard deviation of data's values, the square root of variance; None for an empty slice.

sample_variance fn

The sample variance of data's values, the squared deviations from their mean divided by one less than the count (Bessel's correction); None for fewer than two values.

For values that are the whole population, use variance.

sample_stddev fn

The sample standard deviation of data's values, the square root of sample_variance; None for fewer than two values.

median fn

The median of data's values: the middle one of them sorted, or the mean of the two middle ones when the count is even; None for an empty slice.

The values are copied, converted to f64 and sorted as Vec::sort sorts floats (every NaN after every number); data is not changed.

percentile fn

The pth percentile of data's values, p from 0 to 100, with linear interpolation between the two sorted values it falls between; None for an empty slice.

The position is (count - 1) · p / 100 in the sorted values (R's type 7, the default of spreadsheets and NumPy): percentile(data, 0.0) is the minimum, percentile(data, 100.0) the maximum, and percentile(data, 50.0) the median. Faults (assert_failed) when p is below 0, above 100 or a NaN.

minimum fn

The smallest of data's values as an f64; None for an empty slice.

A NaN is passed over: the result is a NaN only when every value is one.

maximum fn

The largest of data's values as an f64; None for an empty slice.

A NaN is passed over: the result is a NaN only when every value is one.

describe fn

The count, minimum, maximum, mean, stddev and median of data's values as one Summary; None for an empty slice.

std::time impl/std/time.cb

DateTime struct

A moment in UTC: a date of the proleptic Gregorian calendar and a time of day to the second.

year 0 is 1 BC and -1 is 2 BC; there are no leap seconds, so every day has 86,400 seconds. Any field values can be written in a struct literal: DateTime::new checks them, and DateTime::to_unix faults on a value that names no moment. Keep moments in UTC and convert with DateTime::to_local only for display.

DateTime::from_unix fn

The moment s seconds after 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, or before it when s is negative.

Every i64 names a moment, so this never fails.

DateTime::now fn

The moment now by the wall clock, to the second: DateTime::from_unix(unix_seconds()).

DateTime::new fn

The DateTime with these fields, or None when they name no moment.

None for a month 13, a 30 February, a 29 February in a common year, an hour 24 or a second 60. A leap year is divisible by 4 and not by 100, or by 400.

DateTime::to_unix fn

The seconds from 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z to the moment t, negative before it; the inverse of from_unix.

Faults (invalid_datetime) when the fields of t name no moment, or when the count does not fit in an i64.

DateTime::weekday fn

The day of the week of the date of t.

Defined for every valid t, however far from 1970. Faults (invalid_datetime) when the date of t names no day.

DateTime::to_iso fn

The moment in ISO 8601 form in UTC, such as 2026-10-03T10:17:00Z.

Each field is zero-padded to its width. A year outside 0 ..= 9999 is written with its sign and at least four digits (-0001, +10000). Use iso_from_unix_ms for a timestamp with milliseconds.

DateTime::from_iso fn

Reads a moment in to_iso's form, or a date alone (YYYY-MM-DD) as its midnight.

The year is four digits, or a sign and four or more. The seconds may carry a fraction (:37.25Z), which is dropped; unix_ms_from_iso keeps it to the millisecond. No other form is read.

  • Err(Empty) for the empty text.
  • Err(Invalid(i)): byte i is the first that does not fit the form (the length when the text stops short).
  • Err(OutOfRange): the fields name no moment (a month 13, a 29 February in a common year, a second 60), or the year is beyond i64.

DateTime::eq fn

Whether a and b are the same moment, every field equal.

DateTime::less fn

Whether a is earlier than b, comparing the fields in order of significance.

For valid values this is the order of to_unix. It fits Vec::sort_by.

DateTime::to_local fn

The moment t, given in UTC, written in the machine's local time.

The result is a DateTime like any other and knows nothing of its zone: print its fields, not to_iso (which writes Z), and keep the UTC value for arithmetic, since to_unix of the result is the moment plus the offset. Faults (invalid_datetime) when t names no moment, or when the moment is within a day of an i64 limit.

DateTime::to_http_date fn

The moment in HTTP's date form, such as Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT.

The form (RFC 9110 §5.6.7, the IMF-fixdate) is what the Date, Last-Modified and Expires headers carry. Faults (invalid_datetime) for a year outside 0 ..= 9999, or fields that name no moment.

DateTime::from_http_date fn

Reads an HTTP date in any of the three forms a recipient must accept (RFC 9110 §5.6.7).

The forms are Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT (the one to send), the obsolete RFC 850 Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT (a two-digit year: 70 to 99 are 1970 to 1999, 00 to 69 are 2000 to 2069) and asctime's Sun Nov 6 08:49:37 1994. The words are separated by ASCII whitespace; the weekday is not checked against the date.

  • Err(Empty) when the text has no words.
  • Err(Invalid(i)): i is the start of the first word that does not fit.
  • Err(OutOfRange): the fields name no moment.

Weekday enum

A day of the week, Monday to Sunday.

Weekday::text fn

The day's English name (Monday).

unix_ms fn

The wall clock in milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, rounded down.

unix_ms() / 1000 is unix_seconds() when read together. The wall clock may be changed while the program runs; measure elapsed time with monotonic_ns.

local_offset_seconds fn

How many seconds the machine's local time is ahead of UTC at the moment unix seconds after 1970.

Negative when local time is behind UTC; daylight saving included, by the operating system's rule for the zone the program runs in. Between -64800 and 64800. For a moment the system has no rule for, the offset now. It differs between machines, and on one machine between moments.

monotonic_ns fn

Nanoseconds on a monotonic clock, from a start fixed for the whole program.

The clock never goes backwards, so the difference of two readings measures how long something took. Its values mean nothing else; use unix_ms for the time of day.

unix_seconds fn

The wall clock: whole seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z.

The wall clock may be changed while the program runs; measure elapsed time with monotonic_ns.

sleep_ms fn

Makes the calling thread do nothing for at least ms milliseconds; other threads run meanwhile.

iso_from_unix_ms fn

The moment ms milliseconds after 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z in to_iso's form, with milliseconds.

The form is 2026-10-07T12:34:56.789Z, a log line's or a JSON document's timestamp. A negative ms is before 1970, the milliseconds still counted forward within their second.

unix_ms_from_iso fn

The milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z of a moment in DateTime::from_iso's form.

A fraction of the seconds is kept to the millisecond: its first three digits, fewer filled with zeros, further digits ignored (.5 is 500, .1234 is 123). The errors are from_iso's; Err(OutOfRange) also when the milliseconds do not fit in an i64.

std::process impl/std/process.cb

Command struct

A program to run: its name or path, its arguments, its working directory and its environment.

Made by Command::new, changed by arg, current_dir, env and clear_env, and run by output, output_with_input, status or spawn, any number of times. No shell is involved: each argument reaches the program exactly as given, with no splitting, quoting or expansion; a program that wants a shell runs one by name (/bin/sh with -c).

Running fails with Err(NotFound) when there is no such program, Err(Denied) when it may not be run, and Err(Io) for any other failure to start it (a working directory that does not exist among them).

Command::new fn

A command running program with no arguments, in this program's working directory and environment.

A name without a separator is looked for on PATH, as the system does.

Command::arg fn

Appends one argument, passed to the program exactly as given.

Command::current_dir fn

Sets the working directory the program starts in.

A directory that does not exist makes the run fail with Err(Io).

Command::env fn

Sets the environment variable name to value for the program.

The variables set this way go on top of the inherited environment, or of an empty one after Command::clear_env.

Command::clear_env fn

Makes the program start with no environment variables but those Command::env sets.

Command::output fn

Runs the program to its end with an empty standard input, and gives its status and everything it wrote.

Both streams are read at once, so neither pipe fills and stops the program.

Command::output_with_input fn

Runs the program to its end with input as its standard input, as Command::output does.

Command::status fn

Runs the program to its end with this program's standard input, output and error, and gives its status.

The status is Output::status's: the exit code, or on Unix minus the signal that ended it.

Command::spawn fn

Starts the program and returns at once, its three streams pipes to this program.

Output struct

How a run of Command::output ended, and everything the program wrote.

  • status: the exit code, or on Unix minus the number of the signal that ended it (-9 for SIGKILL).
  • stdout: every byte the program wrote to its standard output.
  • stderr: every byte the program wrote to its standard error.

Child struct

A running child process, its standard input, output and error each a pipe to this program.

Made by Command::spawn. Destroying a Child closes its pipes but does not end it: a running child runs on. A child that fills a pipe nobody reads stops until it is read. Child::take_input and Child::take_output move its pipes out, for use from other threads.

Child::id fn

The operating system's number for the child (its process id).

Child::write_input fn

Writes all of data to the child's standard input.

Err(Io) when the child has ended or closed its input; it never ends this program. Does nothing once Child::take_input has taken the input.

Child::close_input fn

Closes the child's standard input, so that the child reads its end.

Does nothing once Child::take_input has taken the input.

Child::read_output fn

Appends to buf what has arrived on the child's standard output, up to max bytes, and returns how many.

Waits for at least one byte; at most a MiB is read at a time. Ok(0) (for a max above 0) means the end of the output.

Child::read_output_line fn

The next line of the child's standard output, without its '\n' or a '\r' just before it.

Ok(None) at the end of the output; Err(Utf8(e)) for a line that is not UTF-8.

Child::read_error fn

Appends to buf what has arrived on the child's standard error, as Child::read_output does.

What Child::read_error_line has read ahead comes first.

Child::read_error_line fn

The next line of the child's standard error, as Child::read_output_line reads standard output.

Each stream is read ahead on its own.

Child::wait fn

Closes the child's standard input, waits for the child to end and gives its status.

The status is Output::status's. Asked again, it gives the same status.

Child::try_wait fn

The child's status if it has ended, without waiting.

Ok(None) while it runs.

Child::kill fn

Ends the child at once (SIGKILL on Unix, TerminateProcess on Windows).

Child::wait then gives its status. Nothing happens to a child that has already ended. Use Child::terminate to let the child stop cleanly, and Child::kill_tree to end the processes it started too.

Child::kill_tree fn

Ends the child and every process it started, and theirs in turn.

On Linux the processes are found from /proc; on Windows by taskkill /T; elsewhere only the child is ended, as Child::kill ends it. Child::wait then gives its status.

Child::terminate fn

Asks the child to end: SIGTERM on Unix, which a program may catch to stop cleanly.

On Windows it ends the child as Child::kill does. On Unix the status Child::wait then gives is -15, unless the child handles the signal. Nothing happens, and Ok(()) is returned, for a child that has already ended.

Child::drop fn

Closes the child's pipes when its Child is destroyed, leaving the child running.

The destructor; programs do not call it.

Child::take_input fn

The child's standard input, moved out of the Child.

Child::write_input and Child::close_input then do nothing. None when the input was taken or closed already.

Child::take_output fn

The child's standard output, moved out of the Child with whatever was read ahead.

Child::read_output then finds the end. None when the output was taken already.

ChildInput struct

A child's standard input as a value of its own, taken out of its Child by Child::take_input.

It is independent of the Child and of the child's output, and outlives the Child, so one thread can write a child's input while another reads its output (or one child's output can feed another's input). Destroying it closes the pipe, and the child reading its input then finds its end.

ChildInput::write fn

Writes all of data to the child's standard input, as Child::write_input does.

ChildInput::drop fn

Closes the pipe when its ChildInput is destroyed, so the child reads the end of its input.

The destructor; programs do not call it.

ChildOutput struct

A child's standard output as a value of its own, taken out of its Child by Child::take_output.

It is independent of the Child and of the child's input, and outlives the Child. Destroying it closes the pipe.

ChildOutput::read fn

Appends to buf what has arrived on the child's standard output, up to max bytes, and returns how many.

As Child::read_output: at most a MiB at a time, and Ok(0) (for a max above 0) only at the end.

ChildOutput::read_line fn

The next line of the child's standard output, as Child::read_output_line reads it.

ChildOutput::drop fn

Closes the pipe when its ChildOutput is destroyed.

The destructor; programs do not call it.

process_id fn

The operating system's number for this program (its process id), as a pid file records it.

watch_interrupts fn

From now on, makes an interrupt set the flag interrupt_requested reads instead of ending the program.

An interrupt is SIGINT or SIGTERM on Unix; Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break or closing the console on Windows. A blocking std call an interrupt arrives in may return early (accept and a socket's read give Err(TimedOut)), so a long-running loop checks the flag and stops cleanly. There is no callback.

interrupt_requested fn

Whether an interrupt has arrived since watch_interrupts was called.

exit built in fn

Ends the program with exit status status ([Exit], spec/21 §2k, D-0150). The calling thread unwinds first, so its destructors run and standard output is written out; other threads are not waited for. The result type is never, so a branch that calls exit needs no value of its own. fn main() : u8's return value is the ordinary way to set the status; exit is for deep inside a program.

std::net impl/std/net.cb

IpAddr enum

An IP address: IPv4 (V4, four bytes) or IPv6 (V6, sixteen bytes).

The bytes are in the order the text writes them: 127.0.0.1 is V4([127, 0, 0, 1]).

IpAddr::localhost_v4 fn

The IPv4 loopback address, 127.0.0.1.

IpAddr::unspecified_v4 fn

The IPv4 unspecified address, 0.0.0.0.

A listener bound to it accepts connections to any of the machine's IPv4 addresses.

IpAddr::localhost_v6 fn

The IPv6 loopback address, ::1.

IpAddr::unspecified_v6 fn

The IPv6 unspecified address, ::.

IpAddr::parse fn

Reads an IP address from its text, as the platform's library does.

Accepts dotted decimal (127.0.0.1) and RFC 4291 IPv6 with :: (::1, 2001:db8::8a2e:370:7334, ::ffff:192.0.2.1), without brackets or a port. Err(Empty) for "", Err(Invalid(0)) for any other text that is not an address.

IpAddr::text fn

The address as text: dotted decimal, or IPv6 in RFC 5952's shortest form (::1).

SocketAddr struct

An IP address and a port: where a socket is bound or connected.

SocketAddr::new fn

The socket address of ip and port.

SocketAddr::parse fn

Reads an address and a port written a.b.c.d:port or [v6]:port.

  • Err(Empty) for "".
  • Err(Invalid(i)) at the first byte that does not fit; i is the address's first byte when the address is not one (an IPv6 address must be in brackets, an IPv4 address must not).
  • Err(OutOfRange) for a port above 65535.

SocketAddr::text fn

The address and port as text, in the forms SocketAddr::parse reads: 127.0.0.1:8080, [::1]:8080.

NetError enum

Why a socket operation failed.

  • Refused: nothing listens at the address connected to.
  • Reset: the peer reset the connection.
  • TimedOut: the socket's timeout passed; the socket is still usable.
  • Unreachable: the address cannot be reached.
  • AddrInUse: the address to bind is already in use.
  • AddrNotAvailable: the address to bind cannot be used on this machine.
  • UnknownHost: the name resolves to nothing or cannot be resolved.
  • NotPermitted: the system denied permission.
  • Closed: the peer has gone while writing, or a read_exact was cut short.
  • Failed: any other failure.
  • NotUtf8(e): a line read_line read is not UTF-8.

No variant shares a name with FileError's, so either may be written unqualified.

NetError::text fn

A short description of the error, in lower case, for messages.

TcpListener struct

A socket that listens for TCP connections; accept gives each one as a TcpStream.

Dropping it closes the socket.

TcpListener::bind fn

Listens for TCP connections at a.

Port 0 asks the system for a free port, which local_addr names. Err(AddrInUse), Err(AddrNotAvailable) or Err(NotPermitted) when the address cannot be bound.

TcpListener::local_addr fn

The address the listener is bound to, with the port the system chose when bind asked for port 0.

TcpListener::set_accept_timeout_ms fn

Sets how long accept waits for a connection, in milliseconds; 0 waits for ever.

After the timeout accept gives Err(TimedOut) and the listener is still usable. A server loop that checks interrupt_requested() sets one.

TcpListener::accept fn

Waits for the next connection made to the listener and gives its stream.

Err(TimedOut) when the accept timeout (set_accept_timeout_ms) passes first.

TcpListener::drop fn
